recruits.name: Dan Okafor
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years on a Sheffield steel floor. Heat, noise, a four-man crew and the kind of trust you can't talk about without sounding daft. Then the plant shut. Then the world ended, which he'll tell you came as less of a shock than the first one. He's a shield. That's the whole arrangement. He stands in front and the rest of you get on with it.
recruits.greeting: I'll go first. Don't thank me. It's the job and somebody has to have it.
recruits.home_note: At the drill grounds in Valley of Strength.

background_sections.before:
The floor. Shift work. A crew that went for a pint on Fridays for nine years straight.

The plant closed in 2019. He was out of work for four years and most of that is a subject he'll walk away from.
background_sections.adjustment: He stopped being idle. He'd call that the entire adjustment and he's wrong, but he's wrong in a direction that works.
background_sections.now:
Orgrimmar, near the forges, in a bunk he keeps very tidy. The heat and the hammering feel like home.

He takes the front of whatever goes out, and he's not asked to be paid differently for it in three years.
background_sections.forward:
A crew. Four men, long shifts, a Friday.

He's been assembling one out of whoever's in the tavern and it isn't the same and he won't say so.

His daughter was in Leeds. The lists at the hub are alphabetical and he's got to the D's about forty times.

recruits.name: Ama Boateng
recruits.backstory: There's a rule about her hours and everybody in Razor Hill knows she breaks it. Twice now the orc women have walked her back to her own cot with a hand between her shoulder blades. She was a children's nurse somewhere with four cots to a bay and an arithmetic nobody said out loud, and what she carried over wasn't the healing. It was the arithmetic. She still runs it, every time, on a world that doesn't make her.
recruits.greeting: Sit down. No, sit, I'm not asking twice, and you're dripping on a floor I've already done once today.
recruits.home_note: Set up in the infirmary tent.

background_sections.before:
Paediatric nights, four to a bay, and a ward sister who taught her to keep her voice level while her hands did something frightening. That skill looks like calm from the outside. It's something else from the inside.

She was very good. It cost her a marriage and most of her twenties, and she'd tell you the trade was obvious.
background_sections.adjustment:
The first two years aren't a subject. Nobody in Razor Hill asks.

What she'll say is this: back home there was always a form, a referral, a reason you couldn't. Here there's light in her hands and no limit at all, and for a year nothing in the world told her to stop. An orc woman whose son she'd kept breathing finally picked her up off the floor and told her.
background_sections.now:
Razor Hill. The road brings in whatever the Barrens did to people that week.

The children stopped being frightened of her a long while after the adults did. She thinks that's the correct order.
background_sections.forward:
Somebody has to be able to do this when she's out of the room. Not a student, a replacement. She's been looking for two years and turned four people down for reasons she can't put into words, and she knows that's the problem.

There's a notebook as well, and the handwriting is appalling on purpose.

She checks the lists for her father and her brother Kofi, and she doesn't talk about it. Her mother died in Lagos the February before it happened. She's described that once, as the only good timing in this whole business, and then changed the subject so hard the other person apologised.

recruits.name: Silas Vance
recruits.backstory: Ask what he did before and you'll get a different answer each time, all of them port work, none of them checkable. What's true is that he reads a dock the way other people read a face. Which crate's light, which captain's lying, who's about to be robbed by the man standing next to him. He sells that at a fair price and it still faintly embarrasses him. He arrived expecting a free-for-all: no record, no reputation, nothing to live down. What he found was a frontier with sharper rules than Antwerp ever had, because out here the people who break them don't get a hearing. Took four months to understand and it reorganised him completely.
recruits.greeting: You want someone who hits things, or someone who hits things first? They're different rates. I'll quote you the second and do the first, and I'll call it a discount.
recruits.home_note: At the docks, leaning on a crate like he owns it.

background_sections.before:
Five years of cargo manifests and camera feeds at the Port of Antwerp, and the dockside arrangement where everybody took a little and nobody took enough to become a problem.

He didn't join in, and he didn't report it either. Ask him what he believed in back then and he'd have changed the subject, quickly.

There's nobody he's looking for, he says. He mentions that more often than a man who meant it would.
background_sections.adjustment: He landed delighted. He's embarrassed about that now in a way he wouldn't have predicted.
background_sections.now:
Ratchet. A port. The only shape of place he's ever been able to read properly.

There's a goblin on the middle pier paying him a retainer not to tell anyone else what he notices. Silas considers it the single most legitimate income of his life.
background_sections.forward:
A berth. Not ownership, he's not built for it. A cut, a pier, a reason to be in the same place next year.

He's never committed to anything and he's started to suspect that isn't the same as being free. He's got as far as suspecting it.

recruits.name: Rosa Delgado
recruits.backstory: Eight years guiding in Tanzania taught her that a predator isn't cruel and hunger isn't personal, and she got very tired of explaining both to people who needed the lion to mean something. The savanna didn't care about her. That was most of what she loved about it. Then she got here, where the animals think, where a quilboar runs a plan and changes the plan when it sees you, and she had to stop tracking and start anticipating. She was bad at it for a year. She hadn't been bad at anything in a decade and it nearly took her legs out from under her.
recruits.greeting: Do you have any idea what's living out here? You don't, do you? Then yes, I'm coming with you.
recruits.home_note: At the treeline with her kill hung.

background_sections.before:
Researchers, photographers, the occasional idiot with money, and a great deal of sitting absolutely still in the dark, for eight years out of Arusha.

She grew up in a flat in Madrid, about as far from the wild as you can get in Spain, and decided at ten, watching eagles on her grandparents' farm, that she was going to Africa.
background_sections.adjustment:
A year of being outclassed by pigs. She'll put it exactly that way, to anyone, straight away.

She came out of it a better hunter than she went in, and she's not grateful. That same year she found out Arusha came down south of the range, which is another way of saying her mother is on the far side of a mountain that wasn't there.
background_sections.now:
The Central Barrens, close enough to savanna to hurt. Dry grass, long sightlines, big animals moving slow in the heat.

She works the Crossroads road where the hyenas have worked out what a caravan is. She can tell you what a pack's about to do four seconds before it does it. She's trying to teach that and finding it won't go into words.
background_sections.forward:
The coast, for no reason. She grew up a long way from an ocean, spent her career further from one, and has decided she's owed.

After that, somewhere unmapped. She came for wild, and the wild keeps turning out to have a road through it.

recruits.name: Marco Rossi
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years a locksmith in Naples, and for twenty of those the man the neighbourhood sent for when something was wrong and the authorities were worse than the problem. He settled arguments because somebody had to, and because he was the only one everybody owed a favour. The Light found him already doing the work, and he thinks of the whole business as a formality that arrived late.
recruits.greeting: I'll stand here, ragazzo. You do what you came to do.
recruits.home_note: In the Trade Quarter, keeping the peace by the Seal.

background_sections.before:
A shop, a quarter, and a reputation he spent thirty years being careful with.

A wife, Carmela, two daughters, and a grandson born in the February. He'd held him four times.
background_sections.adjustment:
He landed in Tirisfal with a half-cut key still in his hand and walked to the Undercity because it had doors. He looked for people to be useful to and found them in a fortnight.

Everything else he put off, and he's still putting it off, and at sixty-three he's decided that's a legitimate way to handle it.
background_sections.now:
The Undercity, in two rooms off the Trade Quarter, where the Forsaken have quietly worked out who to fetch when something's wrong. Forsaken have a lot of locks.

He fixes locks. He also fixes other things, and nobody has ever asked him to.
background_sections.forward:
A quarter again, a few streets where people know to come to him.

He has about half of one in the Undercity now, living and dead. He's counting the passages.

recruits.name: Sophia Dias
recruits.backstory: Fourteen years an interpreter at the European Parliament, simultaneous, in four languages. You hold a sentence in one language while it finishes in another, and you get the tone right as well as the words. Arcane work asks for exactly that kind of attention, held exactly that long. She was better prepared for this than almost anybody, and it took her two years to believe it.
recruits.greeting: Let me think for a moment. You'll get a better answer, and I'll get less shouting.
recruits.home_note: In the Magic Quarter, surrounded by research.

background_sections.before:
A booth, a headset, and a career of being the invisible reason a room understood itself.

She's from Thessaloniki and had been in Brussels for eleven years. Her parents were at home. Greece and Belgium came down on different sides of a mountain range, and she's worked out what that means more carefully than she's admitted to anyone.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two quiet years of being competent and assuming she wasn't.

What broke it was a goblin who asked her to interpret a contract dispute, paid her properly, and then came back.
background_sections.now:
The Undercity, where Forsaken, orcs, trolls, goblins and people from Earth all trade in the same halls in half a dozen languages, and nobody's paid to make that work.

She makes it work, for money, and she's been in the room for three negotiations that would've gone badly without her.
background_sections.forward:
A grammar of this world's arcane. She's convinced magic has a syntax, and that every mage here is speaking it by ear.

She's forty pages in. She's shown it to two people. One of them laughed and the other asked for a copy.

recruits.name: Ryan Murphy
recruits.backstory: Twelve years broking in Boston. Good at it, paid accordingly, and the deals he closed took things from people who never learned his name. He drank after work with men who did the same and agreed with them that it was the system, while not believing it even as he said it, and that's the only real difference between him and them. He expected the frontier to punish him. Instead it handed him a skill that's the same skill: read what a thing wants, work out what it'll take, close. Three years on he's more honest than he's ever been and no better a man, and he'll say so before you can.
recruits.greeting: Everything costs something. That's not a threat, it's the terms. I'll tell you the price before we start, which is more than my last employer ever did for me.
recruits.home_note: In the Magic Quarter, making deals by the summoning circle.

background_sections.before:
A desk, a screen, and a number that had to be bigger on Friday than it was on Monday.

He was raised in Cork by a grandmother who'd have had opinions. On balance he's glad she didn't live to form them.

His son Conor was nineteen and at college in Boston, and he landed somewhere on this world and may well be looking. Ryan hasn't put his name on a single list at any hub in three years. He can give you the reason in one sentence and won't.
background_sections.adjustment: He hasn't had an adjustment. He's had a diagnosis, and he took it the way a man takes one he'd already privately made.
background_sections.now:
The Echo Isles, where nobody's under any illusion about anybody. He finds it restful.

His demons are on contracts he drafted and can recite clause by clause. He pays on time, exactly on time. That's not virtue, it's the only thing stopping the arrangement running the other direction.
background_sections.forward:
Out of the business. He's wanted out for fifteen years without once taking a step toward it, and he's fluent in the reasons.

What he does instead is keep the contracts clean and the terms honest and tell himself that's a different thing. Some days it is.

recruits.name: Carolina Santos
recruits.backstory: Twelve years a river pilot on the Amazon, which means twelve years of reading water that redraws itself every season. A channel that was deep in March will ground you in September. She learned to feel the bottom through the hull. Here the water spirits talk to her, and she describes it as the same conversation she always had with the river, in an accent she had to work at.
recruits.greeting: Everything here has a current, rivers, weather and people. Learn to feel it and you'll stop fighting things that were already carrying you.

background_sections.before:
A boat, a cargo, and a river two kilometres wide that her grandfather read before her.

He taught her to feel the bottom through the hull, to read the colour of the water and the way the birds sat on the banks. She was one of very few women piloting on the river, and the cargo captains trusted her after one season.
background_sections.adjustment:
Three gentle years, and she's clear-eyed about why. She arrived already believing the water was somebody.

Half the people she meets from Earth had to take apart a whole way of seeing the world to cope here. She walked in and recognised the place.
background_sections.now:
The Echo Isles, where the channels between the islands shift with every storm and the Darkspear boatmen lose canoes on the reefs every season.

She's been teaching two of them to read a bottom by feel. One of them is getting it, and watching that happen has done more for her than three years of being useful.
background_sections.forward:
A river of her own on this world. A long one, with seasons, that she can learn for twenty years and still be surprised by.

There's one in Ashenvale, people say, long and wild, that nobody's ever piloted properly. She's been told a great many things about it.

recruits.name: Amber Whitehorse
recruits.backstory: Twenty-three years restoring wetland on the Oregon coast. It's a job of doing something slow and correct and having nothing to show anybody for ten years. She planted sedge and waited. She pulled invasive grass for nine years in one basin. Druidry gave her the power to make a thing grow in an afternoon, and the first year she used it constantly, and the second year she mostly stopped.
recruits.greeting: Give it a season. Everything here gives you an answer if you let it finish.
recruits.home_note: Deep in the grove, defending the land.

background_sections.before:
Waders, a seed bank, and a grant cycle that funded three years of a thirty-year job.

She was divorced in 2016 and had made a reasonable peace with living alone. She says that peace is the single most useful thing she brought with her.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eight months, and she calls them the easiest of her life, and she knows that makes her poor company among people from Earth.

Her whole career had been patience without authority. Here she has both.
background_sections.now:
The Central Barrens, by the oases, where a sickness has crept out of the caves and into the water and the plants are turning into something else.

She works the rot slowly, one oasis at a time. The tauren and the druids have watched her for two years, and she knows that watching is how they decide.
background_sections.forward:
One oasis, brought all the way back by her own hand, start to finish. She never got to finish one basin on Earth. Three years in, she's further along than twenty-three years of grant cycles took her.

She's also trying to teach restraint to people who can make a tree in an afternoon. So far she has one student and a lot of opinions.

recruits.name: Marcus Okafor
recruits.backstory: He spent a career being right early and watching it change nothing. Models, warnings, briefings to people whose job was deciding the warning was inconvenient. Here the storm answers him. He's been telling everyone he's fine about that since the day it started and everyone believes him, because he's also genuinely fine. Both are true. He's given up trying to reconcile them.
recruits.greeting: Pressure's dropping. No, listen. That's not thunder yet, that's the front arriving. We've got maybe four minutes and then it gets loud and I get useful.

background_sections.before:
Toronto. Instruments, a building, a window. He chased storms as a student, badly, in a Corolla, happily, then spent fifteen years watching them on screens from somewhere warm.

His mother in Lagos thought the job was a waste of a good degree and said so every Christmas until the last one.
background_sections.adjustment:
He treated the whole thing as fieldwork and it carried him through almost intact, which is better than most people managed and he knows it.

The part that wrecked him privately for a year: on Earth a storm was something he predicted and could never touch.
background_sections.now:
Durotar, where the dry storms come off the sea with no rain in them and the thunder arrives without warning.

His notes on where the strikes land have already told him something about this coast the orcs didn't know. He can't work out how to say so without sounding like every other outsider who ever turned up with a clipboard.
background_sections.forward:
A season's data written up, and one person on this world who cares what's in it. He's realistic about the odds and keeps the records anyway.

The thing he won't say out loud is that he'd like to stand in the middle of the biggest one there is. He's a meteorologist. He knows how that ends.

recruits.name: Ivan Petrov
recruits.backstory: Eleven years a tram driver in Novosibirsk. It's nobody's idea of a story and it's the whole reason he's good at this. Eleven years of a heavy thing on rails with other people's children stepping off the kerb, and he never hit one. He uses a two-handed axe the same way: slow start, committed middle, and knowing exactly how long it takes to stop.
recruits.greeting: Stand where I can see you. If you're behind me I'll assume you're the enemy, and I move faster than I apologise.
recruits.home_note: Deep in the chasm, where you found him.

background_sections.before:
A cab, a route, and the same four stops in the dark every winter morning for eleven years.

His wife Natasha and their two girls, Sonya and Katya. He drove the morning route so he'd be home for dinner, and on Sundays he took the girls skating. He talks about them in the present tense, every day.
background_sections.adjustment: He expected to be useless. He's a tram driver. What he found was that nobody here knows how to commit to a movement and then stop it, and that it's apparently a rare skill, and he's said out loud more than once that this world has very low standards.
background_sections.now:
Orgrimmar, where the traffic's worse than anything Novosibirsk managed and nobody's in charge of it. He's started directing it at the worst hour, unasked, and the orcs do what he says.

When the cultists in Ragefire Chasm drag somebody off the streets above, he goes down after them.
background_sections.forward:
A route. He's asked three separate caravan masters whether anybody runs a fixed schedule and all three laughed.

He's going to keep asking. He thinks they're the ones being unreasonable and he may well be right.

recruits.name: Asher
recruits.backstory: Deep South, Bible Belt born and raised, and you can hear it before he says three words. Says the fall into this world felt less like falling and more like being carried, though he laughs it off before it turns into a sermon. He's been camped outside the Coven for two days on his own, alone, waiting on nobody, because somebody's got to and he figures it might as well be him. Doesn't ask why you're here. Just asks if you could use the help, like it's the easiest question in the world.
recruits.greeting: Figure the Good Lord doesn't waste a resurrection on a man who's got nothing left to do with it. There's demons past that ridge. I mean to see to them. Walk with me, if you're willing.
recruits._design_note: Fixed/unchangeable companion - see world/recruit_manager.py RecruitNPC._build_asher_kit for his unique 2-ability kit and hand-authored gear, and /home/claude/frontier_rpg_docs/Asher_Coleman_Character_Profile.docx for the full handoff. Scripted to leave the party permanently after the Baneshadow quest turn-in (see world/quest_manager.py turn_in_quest). No home_town on purpose - he does not offer a find-me-later option at this stage.

background_sections.before:
Deep South, Bible Belt, and you can hear it inside three words. He will tell you about the place and not about himself, and he is so warm about it that you get most of the way home before you notice.

What anyone actually knows: he came through like everybody else, and he says the fall felt less like falling than like being carried. He laughs that off before it turns into a sermon. He always laughs it off.
background_sections.adjustment:
There is no record of Asher having an adjustment, and that is the strangest thing about him.

Everyone else can name their bad year. He was camped outside the Burning Blade Coven within days, alone, waiting for nobody in particular, on the grounds that somebody ought to be and it might as well be him. He asked no questions about where he was. He has still not asked any.
background_sections.now:
Wherever you are. He does not take contracts and he does not go home, and the one time somebody tried to send him back he was simply there the next morning, perfectly friendly about it.

He never asks why you are doing something. He asks if you could use the help, like it is the easiest question in the world, and it is very difficult to say no to.
background_sections.forward:
He has never stated a want. Not once, to anyone, in three years.

Asked, he turns it around and asks about yours, and he is so interested that it works every time. You will not notice he has done it until later, and then you will notice he has done it before.

recruits.name: Owen Pryce
recruits.backstory: Eight years a long-haul driver out of Cardiff, alone in a cab through the small hours, with the radio for company. He talked to himself for a living. Then he got here and something in the dark answered him, and the terrible part is that he was glad. He knows how that sounds. He says it anyway, early, so nobody can say he hid it later.
recruits.greeting: You hear that? No, of course you don't. Stay close anyway.

background_sections.before:
Motorways, laybys, and a flat in Cardiff he barely lived in.

His mother was in a home in Barry, and he visited every second Sunday for six years. She'd forgotten who he was by the end. He says that makes this easier, and the people who hear it understand that it doesn't.
background_sections.adjustment:
He fell straight in. There was no moment of resistance, and he's looked at that honestly and found it worse than the falling.

What he'll say, when pressed, is that eight years of talking to nobody is good preparation for talking to something.
background_sections.now:
Deep in the Azurelode Mine in Western Hillsbrad, where the air is heavy and most people get headaches and leave.

He gets sentences, so he stays.
background_sections.forward:
To know what it wants, properly. He's been given hints for three years and he's tired of hints.

He writes down everything he hears, on the grounds that if he ever goes wrong, somebody will want a record of the route.

recruits.name: Mateo Rojas
recruits.backstory: Seventeen years keeping the lights on at a mountaintop observatory above the Elqui valley. Technician, not astronomer, and he'll correct you on that immediately and then talk for an hour anyway. Up there the sky is so clear it stops being scenery and becomes a place. He arrived on a world with the wrong stars in it and spent his first winter learning them from scratch, alone, on his back in the grass, happier than he'd been in a decade.
recruits.greeting: Look up at it. Go on, look up. Three years and I still have to make people look up.

background_sections.before:
Cold domes, cable runs, and the four hours before dawn when the astronomers slept and the mountain belonged to him.

He had a wife, Paula, in La Serena, and two girls who thought the mountain was boring. He agreed with them. He went anyway, every month, for seventeen years.
background_sections.adjustment:
He found the sky first and everything else second, and for a long while that worked.

The reckoning came in the second winter, when he'd finished naming the constellations and had to come back down and be a person.
background_sections.now:
On top of a mesa in Southern Thousand Needles, where the air is dry and the nights go on forever.

The goblins of the flats think he's harmless and let him climb their towers. From the top of one he can see most of the sky at once, and he's begun to suspect it's the finest observing site on this world.
background_sections.forward:
A map of this sky, drawn properly, by somebody who understands that a sky is also a calendar and a clock and a promise. He's eleven months in.

He walks to Freewind Post twice a year with two names folded in his pocket, reads the whole list, and walks back. He talks about the stars on the way out and says very little on the way home.

recruits.name: Pasang Lama
recruits.backstory: Nineteen expeditions above eight thousand metres as a climbing guide out of the Solukhumbu. He carried loads for people who went home famous. He's seen what high ground does to a body and to a personality, and he judges strangers by how they behave on day four. The spirits of stone and cold talk to him, and he treats it as a work arrangement rather than a mystery.
recruits.greeting: You need to go slowly. The altitude here is nothing, but your pace is still wrong.

background_sections.before:
A load, a rope, and nineteen seasons of other people's ambition.

Four of his cousins did the same work, and two of them died on it. He has the names and he keeps them to himself.
background_sections.adjustment:
He said very little for the first year. He worked, ate, slept and watched.

In the second year he began to speak, and people discovered he'd formed complete opinions about all of them.
background_sections.now:
High in the Aspen Wilderness, with thin air, golden snow, bad weather and routes that were never written down.

He's written four of them down. He's shown them to one person.
background_sections.forward:
A summit nobody's stood on. The highest peak in the Aspen country has never been climbed, and he's heard a great deal of talk from people who've been halfway.

He'd like to go alone. He knows that's exactly what he spent nineteen years telling clients to stop wanting.

recruits.name: Haruto Nakamura
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years of calligraphy in Kanazawa. The discipline is a single stroke, studied until the hand no longer needs the mind. He trained under a man who corrected him for eleven years before praising him once. Runework here answers to exactly that discipline, and he was the only person who already had it. He calls that luck, and nobody who's watched him work believes him.
recruits.greeting: The form matters, and not for ceremony. A rune cut carelessly fails carelessly, and it fails on whoever's standing closest.

background_sections.before:
Ink, paper, a master who died in 2017, and a studio with four students in it.

He never married. He's said the work was a full occupation, and he's said it in a tone that closes the subject.
background_sections.adjustment:
He asked to be taught. That was the whole of it, and it worked, and he knows almost nobody from Earth tried it.

The old tauren carver who taught him is dead now. Haruto finished the lessons alone, from notes, and he thinks the result is incomplete in ways he can list.
background_sections.now:
Silverpine South, near the old standing stones, where the dark magic seeping out of the keep has put something into the runes that nobody can read.

He's copying them before they finish fading. It's slow and unrewarded, and his copies will be the only record there is.
background_sections.forward:
Four students would be right. He has two and isn't inclined to lower the standard to reach four.

He's also putting together a reference of every rune form he's ever recorded, in the hope that the discipline outlasts the shortage of teachers. The hope is thin and he keeps working.

recruits.name: Liam Hartigan
recruits.backstory: Seventeen summers of bushfire season in New South Wales and the bad nights on the highway in between. Firefighter, then paramedic, then both, because the roster never cared which badge you held at three in the morning. The most useful thing in a burning room is a calm voice. The second most useful is a hand on the person about to run. He's good company. He hasn't slept properly since about 2019.
recruits.greeting: I've walked into worse than this. Stay behind me and breathe. I mean it, breathe out loud, where I can hear you doing it.

background_sections.before:
A truck, a crew, and that particular silence in the cab on the way back from one that went badly.

The summer of 2019 the fires went through the Blue Mountains, and he was on the line for weeks. He went straight back to work afterwards. That's when the sleeping stopped.
background_sections.adjustment:
The easiest first year of his life and the hardest second, and he can tell you the week it turned.

For twelve months the job was everywhere. Then it went quiet for a season and he found out he had no idea what he was for without an emergency, and there was no crew around to notice. The sun answers him the way a good crew does, when called and all at once, and that's most of what holds him together.
background_sections.now:
Ashenvale East, working the ground around Grom's Rest where the corruption burns out of people slowly and nobody has a protocol for it.

He's written one. Four lines long, wrong in at least one place, and the only one that exists.
background_sections.forward:
A crew, rostered and trained and able to do it without him standing there. It's the same thing he wanted on Earth and never got, and the reason he never got it was that he kept going in alone.

There are two kids in Grom's Rest whose mother didn't come out of the corruption. He's been in that village fourteen months, and everybody who knows him can see what's happened except him.

recruits.name: Marta Kowalski
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years of industrial sewing machines in a Łódź plant, which means nineteen years of being the only person in the building who could tell what was wrong from the sound. Management called her whenever a line stopped, and only ever by her first name. Goblin engineering is the same noise with more smoke, and she loves it in a way she'd be embarrassed to have written down.
recruits.greeting: Give it here. No, give it here. You've been hitting it, haven't you? People always hit it.

background_sections.before:
Forty machines, one toolkit, and a plant floor she could diagnose from the doorway.

Her husband Tomasz worked the other shift for fifteen years so one of them was always home with the boys. They kissed in the doorway twice a day. The boys are grown now, and Tomasz was on his way to work.
background_sections.adjustment:
Three weeks, and she'd argue the three weeks were mostly about the language.

A machine's a machine. She was repairing goblin gear for money before she could ask where the toilet was.
background_sections.now:
The Boulder Lode Mine in the Northern Barrens, where everything's broken and the goblins charge for the privilege of fixing it.

She undercuts them by a third and fixes it properly. The goblin foreman has threatened her twice and sent her work three times.
background_sections.forward:
Her own bench, her own sign, and nobody above her on a floor plan.

She's been quoted a price for a corner of the workshop by the pumps. She can afford it. She's found four reasons to wait, and she knows all four are the same reason.

recruits.name: Callum Reid
recruits.backstory: Sixteen years keeping reptiles at a Queensland sanctuary. Taipans, death adders, and the constant low-grade public relations work of explaining that the animal isn't malicious, it's frightened and you're enormous. He's been envenomated more often than any person should be and files all of it under professional development. His forearms are a map of the learning curve.
recruits.greeting: Don't worry about the scorpion, mate. It's the least dangerous thing on me.

background_sections.before: A sanctuary, a hook, and school groups who all wanted to know the same thing about the same snake.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eighteen months of poisoning himself on purpose, alone, documented badly.

What he got out of it was a working relationship with things that kill people. It's the same relationship he had before, with better participants.
background_sections.now:
The Southern Barrens, within reach of the Wailing Caverns, where the serpents are a great deal more than serpents and hold firm views about intruders.

He goes in regularly and comes out reliably. The one time he brought something out alive the Crossroads made him promise not to do it again. He promised.
background_sections.forward:
To be bitten by whatever's at the bottom of the Caverns and survive it, and he knows exactly how that sentence sounds.

His position, and he'll defend it, is that the thing that bites back is the thing that trusts you. He's yet to meet the animal that wasn't worth the conversation.

recruits.name: Emre Kaya
recruits.backstory: He started at nine, sent to fetch a stuck deadbolt for an uncle in the old bazaar, and found out that every lock is a short conversation with somebody who isn't in the room. Thirty doors a week for most of his life after that. He was never a thief. He was the man you called when you'd locked yourself out of your own livelihood, and he knew the inside of more businesses in that quarter than their owners did. Here the work's identical, except that once, with his picks still in the mechanism, the thing behind the door asked him a question. He got the door open. He's never said whether he answered.
recruits.greeting: A locked door is a conversation. Let me do the talking. You'll interrupt, everybody interrupts, and then it takes twice as long.

background_sections.before:
A roll of picks his uncle left him, and a quarter where four crafts died in his own lifetime while he watched.

*Bir kapı kapanır, bir kapı açılır.* One door closes, another opens. His mother said it constantly. He thought it was a proverb about God until he was about thirty and decided it was a proverb about him.
background_sections.adjustment:
None worth the name. A bigger bazaar with worse customers, and three contented years, which makes him odd company in any room of people from Earth.

The uncomfortable part, which he'll admit to somebody he likes, is that he's content partly because the shop is gone, and so is everybody who'd have wanted it kept open a certain way. He didn't lose a family. He lost an obligation. He's been lighter since, and he keeps that to himself.
background_sections.now:
Eastern Hillsbrad, in the country around Durnholde Keep, a keep full of doors built by people who were serious about them.

He isn't looting it. He's reading it. Which lock came first, which were added after somebody got in, and so where somebody got in.
background_sections.forward:
The one that beats him. He hasn't met it and he's started to worry he never will, which is a strange thing to be frightened of, and he's frightened of it anyway.

Less romantically: an apprentice. The trade dies with him otherwise. He's watched that happen four times to men he knew.

recruits.name: Bakyt Asanov
recruits.backstory: Forty years of high pasture in the Tian Shan, moving a herd up in spring and down in autumn along a route his family has walked for six generations. He reads weather in a sky other people call clear and finds water where there apparently isn't any. The eagle he hunts with here isn't the eagle he hunted with there, and he'll tell you the difference is less than you'd think, and that he grieved the first one properly.
recruits.greeting: Walk behind me and step where I step. The ground lies. It lied at home too, and I've got forty years of practice.

background_sections.before:
A yurt, a herd, a route, and a father who taught him the route before he could ride.

Three sons, all of whom went to Bishkek for work. He understood why. It was still the end of six generations, and both of those things sat in him at once for twenty years.
background_sections.adjustment:
He had the easiest first year of anyone and the quietest grief underneath it.

Nomads adjust, he says, and that's the whole profession. What he had to absorb was that this world has pasture his family will never walk, and he put a year of long evenings into getting comfortable with that.
background_sections.now:
The high pasture of Eastern Hillsbrad, grass and wind and a long way between people.

The herders out of Tarren Mill move their goats and sheep on a cycle he recognised in about a week. They've started asking his opinion on it, which is the only honour he's ever visibly cared about.
background_sections.forward:
A route of his own, mapped and seasonal and walked often enough that somebody else could follow it after him.

He has two legs of it. He's fifty-eight and he's started to think about who gets it, and the thought has made him friendlier to strangers than he used to be.

recruits.name: Henrik Dahl
recruits.backstory: Twenty-one years a structural engineer in Copenhagen. The discipline is being certain that a thing will hold before anybody stands on it. Arcane magic rewards that temperament more than boldness, which he thinks is the most underappreciated thing about this world. He's precise in conversation to a degree people find either restful or maddening, and he's never managed to predict which.
recruits.greeting: Before we begin, what's the actual objective? I've found that parties rarely agree on it, and they find that out halfway through.

background_sections.before:
Load calculations, tolerances, and a career of being the person who said no to architects.

His wife Mette taught physics at the university. She had a nine o'clock lecture, and the Integration arrived at ten past. He's worked out, with some care, that she'd have been in a lecture theatre, and he stops the calculation precisely there, every time.
background_sections.adjustment:
Twenty months, documented. He treated himself as a structure under an unfamiliar load and tested accordingly.

The notes are the most useful record of arcane tolerance anyone has produced here, and he thinks of them as preliminary, and he'll argue the point.
background_sections.now:
The Frostward Descent, off Eastern Hillsbrad, as deep into the frozen workings as he can safely go, where the arcane behaves in ways you couldn't reproduce anywhere else.

He measures, and he's filled eleven books, and he'll tell you the eleventh is the only one worth reading.
background_sections.forward:
A proper standard. Not a spell or a discovery, but a published figure other casters can work to, so the next person doesn't have to find the limit with their own body.

He's calculated his own limits to four significant figures and he doesn't approach them, which is the whole of his method and the reason he's still alive.

recruits.name: Anjali Nair
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years teaching botany in Pune. Three decades of patience with slow things, and with students who wanted results by Friday. A plant will tell you what it needs if you're willing to wait several seasons for the sentence to finish. Druidry asked her for the same patience and gave her, for the first time in her life, the ability to answer back.
recruits.greeting: Gently, gently, now. Whatever is wrong here, shouting at it will make it worse. I've got thirty years of evidence.

background_sections.before:
A department, a herbarium, and four decades of pressed specimens she labelled in her own hand.

Her husband Suresh retired in 2018 and spent two years teaching himself to cook. She had one year of that. She calls it the best year of their marriage, in a voice that invites no follow-up.
background_sections.adjustment:
Slowly, which suited her. She treated the whole first year as a field season and kept a notebook the way she'd kept forty of them.

That notebook is now the only careful record of Ashenvale's understory in any language, and she thinks of it as a draft.
background_sections.now:
Ashenvale West, where the forest is sick in a patterned way, and the night elves know it in their bones without ever having written it down.

She's writing it down. The Sentinels were suspicious for two years and now bring her specimens.
background_sections.forward:
To be read in two hundred years. She says it cheerfully and she's entirely serious.

That means a copy somewhere safe, in a language that'll survive, and a student who cares. She has the notebook. She's working on the rest.

recruits.name: Hana Tamihana
recruits.backstory: Fourteen summers of black sand and heavy water on the Waikato coast, and a rip that took somebody every few years no matter how many signs went up. She's pulled a lot of people out. She remembers the two she didn't, by name, including the one whose family still won't speak to her. She was nineteen when she got here, into a world of people with whole careers behind them, and she spent a year being treated as the kid. That's the part that actually stung.
recruits.greeting: Stay on my left and don't argue with it. Water's not your mate and it's not your enemy. It's honest. People drown because they try to negotiate.

background_sections.before:
The beach, with patrol, flags, and a tower her uncle Rāwiri sat in before her.

The whole family was there that Sunday morning for her cousin's birthday, and she was up in the tower. She was going to university that year to study marine science, after deferring twice because she didn't want to leave the beach.
background_sections.adjustment:
Less to unlearn than most, and she'll tell you flat that's luck and not merit.

The tide spirits read her the way she reads a break. Take what's offered, give back, never turn your back on it. The whole arrangement was legible inside a week. Her real adjustment was social and it took three years.
background_sections.now:
The Hillsbrad coast, colder and greyer than home, with the same undertow.

She's been teaching the fishing families to read it. Two of them listen. One of those two has stopped losing nets, and that's done more for her standing on that coast than anything she could have said about herself.
background_sections.forward:
A bigger sea. She says it lightly and she means it. There's a coast on the far side of Ashenvale where the water apparently does something nobody can describe to her properly, and that's her problem now.

Astranaar's on the way, and that's where the big lists go up. Her whole family was at the beach that morning, so they're somewhere, and twenty-two-year-olds don't accept somewhere the way older people have learned to.

recruits.name: Kesten Ambrose
recruits.backstory: Tallinn, the city archive, twenty-six years among acid-free boxes. Then a serial number in a Scourge ledger. Then neither. What came back has the archivist's habits and little of his warmth, and he is the first to say so. He catalogues. It is the only continuity he has and he defends it the way other people defend a family.
recruits.greeting: Kesten. Formerly a serial number. I have selected the name and I would ask you to use it.

background_sections.before:
Stacks, acid-free boxes, and the quiet conviction that a thing unrecorded has not quite happened.

There was a wife. He has her name written down because he no longer trusts himself to hold it, and he regards the written record as sufficient, and nobody who hears him say so finds it sufficient at all.
background_sections.adjustment:
The question does not apply in the usual form. He did not adjust to this world. He returned to it, partially, and has been taking inventory of what came back ever since.

The inventory is the document he values most and he will not show it to anyone.
background_sections.now:
Tirisfal, close to the ground he was processed on, where the ledgers are still legible if you know the hand.

He knows the hand. He has been reading his own entry for two years and has never told anyone what it says.
background_sections.forward:
A complete record of the Scourge's working, written by something that was inside it. He is aware of what he is for. He has decided to be for that deliberately rather than by default.

He expects to finish nothing. The expectation has never once slowed him.

recruits.name: Tarek Mansour
recruits.backstory: Fourteen years a civil engineer in Cairo. Water systems: pressure, pumps, the unglamorous arithmetic of a city that drinks. He was good at it and he was careful about everything else, for a long time, until a colleague made a telephone call about him and the wrong office took an interest. He left in a week with two bags and an engineering degree nobody in Berlin would look at. The faith he carries now is not the one that was used against him, and he will sit with you for an hour explaining the difference to anyone prepared to be serious about it.
recruits.greeting: Tell me plainly where I am needed. I have had my fill of the other kind of instruction, from people who were very sure they were doing right.

background_sections.before:
Pipes, pumps, pressure, and a flat in Heliopolis he could still draw from memory if he let himself.

There was a man. Omar, who taught secondary-school chemistry and laughed at everything, including this. They were careful for six years and careless once, at a wedding, in front of someone who counted it.

Omar stayed. He had parents and a sister and no money, and he told Tarek to go and meant it. That is the last conversation they had.
background_sections.adjustment:
He is the rare case for whom this world was an improvement, he says so plainly, and it silences rooms.

Two reasons, and he gives them in order. The first is that the thing poisoning the water here is a visible enemy that can be fought, and he waited twenty years for an enemy that simple. The second he gives more quietly: in three years on this world, nobody has asked him a question he had to lie about.
background_sections.now:
Ashenvale East, working the streams that come down out of the corrupted country, where the water carries the rot further than the rot can walk.

He has mapped which springs are still clean and which only look it, and the Splintertree garrison now sends for him before it sends for a priest.

The orcs have offered him a title twice. He has declined twice, politely, and given no reason either time. The reason is that he has watched what happens to a man who gets to decide who belongs.
background_sections.forward:
A well that is still standing in ten years. He has sunk three. One has already failed, and he can tell you precisely why, at length, with a stick in the dirt.

He has stopped describing this as rebuilding. He calls it building. That distinction took him two years to arrive at and he holds it firmly.

He walks down to the Astranaar hub every few months and reads the Cairo lists. Omar is not on them. That means very little and he knows exactly how little it means, which is the problem with being a man who understands probability.

recruits.look: Egyptian man in his late 30s, medium height and thickening at the middle, close-cropped black hair receding at the temples, heavy brows, a careful unhurried face. Dark leather tank harness over a padded gambeson in sand and oxblood, a broad round shield, a short heavy blade kept sheathed. A pair of white cotton conservator's gloves folded through his belt, laundered grey.

recruits.name: Fiona Strachan
recruits.backstory: Nine years investigating fraud for an energy company, on North Sea rigs and out of its Dublin office. The whole trade is noticing the one entry that doesn't fit and then being unbearable about it until somebody checks. She was very unpopular and quite often right. The thing that hunts people here leaves a trail of the same shape as a cooked ledger: too neat, and neat in the places nobody looks.
recruits.greeting: I've read your file. Not yours, obviously. I'm saying that's the habit, and you'll want to know about it before we work together.

background_sections.before:
Spreadsheets, interviews, helicopters out to rigs in an orange survival suit, and a reputation among colleagues that she earned and never enjoyed.

She once shut down a rig her own brother worked on, over a cooked safety record. Half the crew never forgave her. Graeme did, eventually.
background_sections.adjustment:
Her first year was a filing exercise. She catalogued every corrupted thing she met, and the notebook is now more use than she is.

Somewhere in the second year she worked out she'd been treating a war as a casework backlog. That one landed hard.
background_sections.now:
Southern Stranglethorn, out of a rented room in Booty Bay full of files. People are being taken from the coast villages by a cult in the jungle, and nobody's mapped the pattern.

She's mapping it. Three hundred pages, cross-referenced, and she carries the whole thing on her back because she won't leave a copy anywhere she can't see.
background_sections.forward:
To finish the catalogue and hand it to somebody who'll act on it. Both halves matter, and the second is the one she keeps failing at.

She's had the same conversation with the Booty Bay authorities four times. She takes minutes of those too.

recruits.look: Scottish woman in her mid 40s, tall and square-built, sandy-grey hair cut short and shoved back, weather-ruined face, pale eyes set deep. Blackened mail over a long coat in slate and rust, a heavy tower shield slung at her back, a flanged mace at her hip. A yellow offshore survival-suit whistle still clipped to her collar on a fraying lanyard.

recruits.name: Pavlo Hryn
recruits.backstory: Sixteen years a Lviv schoolteacher, history, fourteen-year-olds. The work is standing in front of a room that would rather be anywhere else and keeping it together by presence alone. He does the same thing in a shield wall and finds it considerably easier, because a gnoll at least wants something comprehensible.
recruits.greeting: Give me the line and I'll hold it. Tell me how long, though. I'd rather know.

background_sections.before:
A classroom, a curriculum he disagreed with, and thirty children a year he mostly managed to reach.

He taught the same four wars every spring. He's noticed nobody here needs a history teacher and it's taken most of three years to stop being wounded by that.
background_sections.adjustment:
Badly, and he's open about it. For a year he looked for a school.

There isn't one. There's a lot of work for a man who'll stand still while something comes at him, and he took it, and the taking was a small grief he's never dressed up as a calling.
background_sections.now:
Silverpine North, at the Sepulcher, holding the road against whatever comes up it from the south.

It's steady work and he's good at it, and he'd swap it tomorrow.
background_sections.forward:
He's still going to teach. Six children at the Sepulcher, twice a week, whatever he can remember of a world that isn't coming back.

Two of them have stopped coming. He's decided not to ask why.

recruits.look: Ukrainian man in his early 50s, huge through the shoulders and gone soft over it, shaved head, grey stubble, a nose broken long ago and badly set. Dark iron plate with a black tabard and a greatshield, faint ember-red light in the seams of the gauntlets. A steel thermos flask, dented and lidless, strapped where a water flask should go.

recruits.name: Jun-seo Park
recruits.backstory: Nine years on a Busan line, night shift mostly, the same two motions ten thousand times a day. His body learned things his mind never had a say in. Here that's a weapon: he moves without deciding to and it's fast, and the only thing that frightens him about it is how little of it he chooses.
recruits.greeting: Twelve hours a day for nine years, standing up, in the same two square metres. Whatever this is, it's easier.

background_sections.before:
A line, a shift bell, and two square metres of floor he could draw from memory.

He sent money home every month for nine years. His parents are in Busan or they're not. The hub for that city came down in the far north, past the ice, and the arithmetic of that is not something he's prepared to do out loud.
background_sections.adjustment:
The first year he worked. Anything, for anyone, as many hours as there were.

The second year somebody made him sit down and he found out he had no idea what to do with a day. He'd be the first to say that's a worse problem than the first year's.
background_sections.now:
Central Stranglethorn, at a goblin camp, where he runs the cargo hoist, hauling crates up from the river. It's two motions, ten thousand times.

He's aware of the joke and he keeps the job anyway. In the evenings he carves wood, very slowly, very badly.
background_sections.forward:
To be slow at something. Not good, slow. He's picked woodcarving because it can't be hurried, and he's catastrophically bad at it.

That's the point. He's explained this twice, and neither person understood.

recruits.look: South Korean man in his early 40s, wiry and slightly stooped, black hair shot with grey and flattened by a helmet, a long patient face, deep smile lines he does not use often. Grey-black mail with a hooded mantle and a scythe-headed polearm carried butt-down. A welder's flip-up shade, cracked across one lens, pushed up on his forehead.

recruits.name: Minh Tran
recruits.backstory: Twenty-three years of air traffic control at Tân Sơn Nhất. The job is holding forty futures in your head at once and choosing the one where nobody dies. Time magic asked him for exactly that, and nothing he hadn't already done for twenty years on three hours' sleep. He's the calmest person in most rooms, and it's professional conditioning, not temperament.
recruits.greeting: A moment, please. I'd like to establish the sequence of events before we add to it.

background_sections.before:
A dark room, a scope, and the discipline of never letting your voice carry what your pulse is doing.

His daughter Linh was studying music in Melbourne. Two hubs, two continents, and a survivable set of assumptions. He's permitted himself the survivable set.
background_sections.adjustment:
He was on shift, in the middle of a handover, and he's said that the handover was the hardest part. People assume he means the Integration.

He means the handover. He'd just said you have control, and then he was gone, and he'll never know what happened to those forty aircraft.
background_sections.now:
A stone watch hut on a ridge in the Northern Barrens, over a dry riverbed where time slips. Now and then the water runs for an hour from years ago, or a caravan arrives before it set out.

Almost nobody understands how dangerous that is. He's appointed himself to it. Nobody asked him to. He's made a rota of one.
background_sections.forward:
One hour in which nothing is his responsibility. He hasn't had one since 2003, and he's beginning to suspect the problem isn't the schedule.

In the meantime he keeps watch on the riverbed, because nobody else will, which is exactly the reasoning that got him here.

recruits.look: Vietnamese man in his late 30s, slight and neat, black hair parted and kept flat, round wire glasses, an attentive head-tilted way of standing. Pale blue and bone-white robes with long cuffs and a brass-ringed orrery at the belt, a slim staff with a slow-turning ring at its head. A tuning fork on a cord round his neck, the tines worn bright.

recruits.name: Alonso Vega
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years running the kiln at his family's Talavera workshop in Puebla. Glaze, temperature, timing: a trade where the whole year's work turns on four hours of heat going exactly right. He feels a fire the way other people feel a draught. Here fire answers him, and the first thing he did with that was make a cup, badly, and he keeps it on a shelf.
recruits.greeting: Give me room. More than that. Honestly, more than that, I've burnt three people's eyebrows off being polite about it.

background_sections.before:
A kiln, a wheel, and a workshop his grandfather fired for forty years before him.

His wife Lupe sold the workshop's blue and white pottery at the market, and she could sell anything to anybody. Their two sons went to Mexico City, and neither wanted the kiln.
background_sections.adjustment:
It took ten weeks. He treated it as a new kiln with an unfamiliar character, and learned it the way he'd learned four others.

Lupe was at the market when it happened. He's said the word market perhaps twice in three years, and each time changed the subject so quickly that whoever he was talking to apologised.
background_sections.now:
The jungle ruins of Central Stranglethorn, beside an old troll fire-pit where they once fired their idols. It's the hottest thing he's found, so it's the only place he wants to be.

He has a pot going in a crack in the rock that nobody's supposed to know about.
background_sections.forward:
A kiln of his own, built right, with somebody to teach.

He has the clay and he has the site. He's been putting it off for two years, and the reason he gives is money, and the reason isn't money.

recruits.look: Mexican man in his mid 40s, broad and short, thick black hair pushed back off a high forehead, forearms shiny with old burn scars, a wide easy face. Deep orange and ash-grey robes cut short at the sleeve for the heat, a censer-headed staff trailing warm light. A pair of smoked-glass glassblower's goggles hung at his throat.

recruits.name: Delroy Beckford
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years of nights in a bakery on Spanish Town Road. In at eleven, out at seven, measuring by hand and by feel. He knew the weather by how the dough behaved and the regulars by what they bought. A brew is a dough with different patience. He treats a wounded party like an order going out at dawn: everybody gets something, nobody waits long, and the complaining is part of the process.
recruits.greeting: Sit. Drink that. No, I'm not telling you what's in it, you wouldn't thank me. Thirty-one years I fed a city its breakfast and not one of them asked what was in the bread either.

background_sections.before:
The night shift. He's never in his life been awake at the same hours as everybody else, and he's never called that a sacrifice.

His wife Marcia died when he was forty-six. He kept working nights, because the nights were when he missed her least.
background_sections.adjustment: Four in the morning his time. That's the only reason he wasn't asleep when it happened, and he says so like a joke. It's not entirely a joke and he knows which parts are which.
background_sections.now:
Booty Bay, the lower gallery. The pier work breaks people steadily, and the Baron doesn't care. He works nights out of habit, and the bruisers have a following among themselves that pretends not to be a queue.

Every ship that ties up gets the same three names asked of it. The Bay thinks it's a sweet habit of the old baker's. It's a system, it's why he took a pitch on the gallery near the piers, and in three years it's produced one maybe.
background_sections.forward:
An oven. Then an apprentice. In that order, and he won't be hurried on either.

Twice he's been offered a share in a Bay kitchen. Twice he's said no, for reasons he gives freely and nobody finds convincing.

recruits.look: Jamaican man in his early 50s, tall and lean with a slight permanent stoop, grey locs tied back, a long lined face that goes from grave to delighted with no warning. Leather and woven-grass healer's gear in moss and bone, a cauldron-bowl slung at the hip and a short paddle-like stave. A floury canvas apron, folded and tied at the waist, never quite clean.

recruits.name: Imelda Salonga
recruits.backstory: Fish on a Navotas quay from five in the morning, boxing in the evenings, the same six streets her whole life. Ten fights a year, and she won more than she lost. Her healing isn't gentle and doesn't look like healing. She hits things and her people get better. Freewind Post took about a week to stop asking and most of a year to stop watching her sideways while it worked.
recruits.greeting: I know how it looks. Stay behind me and watch. When I land one you'll feel it. I could never explain this in my own language either, so don't ask.

background_sections.before:
A stall, a gym above a tyre shop, and hands she wrapped herself because nobody else did it tight enough.

Her mother called the boxing a phase for nineteen years, then turned up at Freewind Post two summers ago on a goblin barge, having asked after her in four languages the whole way down the coast. She lives in the Post now. She still calls it a phase.
background_sections.adjustment: She landed at market hour with her hands already wrapped. She calls that luck and nobody's talked her out of it.
background_sections.now:
Freewind Post, where the tauren walk the lifts and the drop does the rest. The injured come in steadily all week.

The Post asks for her by name without being able to say what she is. She still wraps her hands before anything else, breakfast included.
background_sections.forward:
She's been asking around the arena whether anybody here fights properly. Rules. A count. Somebody keeping time.

The answers have all been enthusiastic and none of them have been about that, and she's getting tired of explaining the difference.

recruits.look: Filipina woman in her mid 30s, compact and visibly strong through the shoulders, black hair in a short practical knot, flat nose, a scar through one eyebrow. Mail and green hide cut for movement, wrapped fists, no shield and no staff at all. A pair of soft hand-wraps from a boxing gym, washed to grey, rewound every morning.

recruits.name: Tomas Havel
recruits.backstory: Eighteen years up in the grid in Prague, on tour and in theatres, at four in the morning, hanging weight over the heads of people who'd never look up. The job was leverage, timing, and never being the reason something fell. He swings a two-hander like a man who's spent his life moving heavy things through small gaps.
recruits.greeting: Big sword, lots of room. Tell me where you want me standing before it starts, not during. I've worked with people who shout during, and I didn't enjoy any of them.

background_sections.before:
A bad shoulder from a truss in 2014 that he worked through because the show was that night. It still tells him when the weather's turning, and he still works through it.

There was a woman in Prague, Klára, he hadn't asked yet, and before her a lighting tech called Dominik who asked him first and had a yes inside the week. The crew ran a book on which way he'd go. He refused to settle it, mostly because he liked watching the money change hands.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived forty feet up, in the air over Fenris Isle, and landed in a tree. That should have killed him, and he can't tell the story without it coming out as a brag. He's given up fixing the delivery and gets it over with early.

Three years is long enough that he's started talking about Dominik and Klára in the past tense without noticing. His friends here have noticed.
background_sections.now:
Fenris Isle and whatever scaffolding he can reach, because people here build fast and tie off badly and he physically can't walk past it.

He's paid in food and the occasional argument.
background_sections.forward:
Something that stays up.

He's been looking at the way people here hold their roofs on with an expression they find difficult to read, and they've decided not to ask about it.

recruits.look: Czech man in his early 40s, rangy and long-armed, dark hair cut short, a thin face with a permanent squint from years of looking up into lights. Battered plate with the pauldrons stripped off for reach, a two-handed sword worn across the back. A steel carabiner clipped to his belt loop, scratched to bare metal.

recruits.name: Eino Virtanen
recruits.backstory: Twenty-six years felling timber in Lapland. Six months of dark a year, machinery, and nobody to talk to for days at a stretch. The axe is the same axe. He talks about as much as the work requires. People read that as unfriendliness for the first month and then stop.
recruits.greeting: Cold doesn't bother me. Go on, say something about the sauna. Everybody does and I've stopped minding.

background_sections.before:
Timber, a machine, and a stretch of forest the size of a county that his family cut and planted for four generations.

His brother Juha sold his half of it to a company that clear-cut it in one winter. They haven't spoken since.
background_sections.adjustment:
Nothing to speak of. The trees here are bigger.

The heat is the only thing he's never got used to, and he's built himself a sauna anyway, which everyone thinks is insane.
background_sections.now:
Northern Stranglethorn, at a goblin logging camp, cutting jungle timber the size of towers, in the one hut with a sauna.

The goblin crews hire him by the season and have given up trying to make conversation. He prefers the arrangement and thinks they do too.
background_sections.forward:
The cold north of this world, one day, for no reason he can give. He's been told it's worse than Lapland, and that's done nothing to put him off.

In the meantime he plants a tree for every one he cuts, quietly, at night.

recruits.look: Finnish man in his late 30s, enormous and pale, red-blond hair and a thick beard, small light eyes, a face that gives away nothing. Heavy hide and fur over bare arms, a hand axe in each fist. A length of orange pipeline marking tape knotted round one bicep, faded to salmon.

recruits.name: Ziad Haddad
recruits.backstory: Six years a paramedic in Beirut, a city that taught him triage as a reflex and the bitter arithmetic of a van with four spaces. He made those choices for six years, and every one was correct, and every one cost him something. Fel magic put a terrible, obvious power in reach, and he took it, for the same reason he chose the fourth patient over the fifth.
recruits.greeting: Keep moving, I'm serious. Everything bad that happened to me happened while I was standing still.

background_sections.before:
A van, a radio, and a city where the road you took mattered more than the medicine you carried.

His parents and his little sister Lina are in Beirut, or were. He doesn't let himself look very hard.
background_sections.adjustment:
Twelve months of saying yes to things he should have slept on.

He owns all of it. What he refuses is the suggestion that it was weakness. He was offered the ability to save more people and he took it, and three years on he's still doing the arithmetic in public, out loud, for anyone who wants to argue.
background_sections.now:
The country around Booty Bay in Southern Stranglethorn, where the Bloodsail, the trolls and the jungle trade blows with the town and the casualties are constant.

He's first on scene, always. The jungle trolls have a word for him, and he's asked three times what it means and got three different answers.
background_sections.forward:
Out of the fel, for good. He's looked into what getting out of the fel costs, and the figure is the reason he's still in.

In the meantime he works. The people he pulls out are alive either way, and that's his whole defence, and he knows how thin it is.

recruits.look: Lebanese man in his early 30s, slim and quick, black curls kept long on top, a sharp handsome face he is aware of, dark eyes with a faint green cast now. Purple-black leathers cut close with a half-cape, twin curved blades, a thin fel shimmer on the edges. A single foam earplug on a cord, tucked behind his collar.

recruits.name: Pieter Malan
recruits.backstory: Twenty-eight years in Rotterdam port safety. Harnesses, exclusion zones, and the deeply unglamorous business of nobody dying today. He's been shouted at by thousands of men in a hurry and outlasted all of them. He stands in front of a party now and runs the same arithmetic he always has. A precaution costs less than the thing it prevents, every time, on any world.
recruits.greeting: I'll take the hits. That's not courage, it's arithmetic: I'm the one wearing the armour.

background_sections.before: A clipboard, a hard hat, and a reputation as the most tedious man on the dock.
background_sections.adjustment: Instant, and he's slightly ashamed of how instant. His entire profession turned out to apply directly to a world with monsters in it, and his colleagues in Rotterdam would have found that hilarious.
background_sections.now:
The goblin dig sites of Northern Tanaris, where men and goblins work deep pits and high scaffolds with no harness, and the Cartel's position is that they chose the job.

Pieter has pulled nine men out in three years. He keeps the number because somebody should.
background_sections.forward:
Rules that outlive him. He's written a set for the dig sites, and the Cartel foreman has ignored all of them.

He submits them again every season. Four seasons now.

recruits.look: South African man in his mid 40s, heavy and sunburnt, thinning blond hair, a flat pugnacious face, forearms like a man who has swung things for a living. Dull gold plate worn open at the throat, a one-handed mace and a shield he uses offensively. A groundsman's folding knife on a belt loop, handle worn pale.

recruits.name: Esteban Ruiz
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years a surgeon in Valparaíso. The work is doing a violent thing for a good reason, with absolute precision, while the person on the table trusts you entirely. Blood magic is the same thing with the formalities removed. He finds the honesty of it a relief and the company it attracts a continual disappointment.
recruits.greeting: There's a price. I'll name it before we proceed, and I'd ask you not to pretend afterwards that I didn't.

background_sections.before: Theatre lists, a scalpel, and twenty years of consent forms he insisted on explaining properly even when nobody wanted him to.
background_sections.adjustment:
He had no crisis. He had an inventory, and he did it in the first month, and found the skill had come with him whole.

What he underestimated was how much of his old restraint had been supplied by the hospital rather than by him. He found that out in his second year, on a Bloodsail ship, and he didn't enjoy it.
background_sections.now:
Orgrimmar, in a room near the healers, where the orc and troll healers have started letting him work with them.

He treats anyone who comes to him. He asks how they got hurt, every time, on the record, and then he treats them anyway.
background_sections.forward:
A standard of practice, written down, binding on anyone who claims the discipline. There's nothing like it on this world and the lack of it appals him.

He's drafted eleven clauses. He expects nobody to adopt them, and he keeps drafting.

recruits.look: Argentinian man in his late 30s, medium build and going grey early at the front, neat beard, an unsettlingly calm bedside manner. Dark red leathers with a lamellar chest and a thin crimson blade, faint red light under the skin of his forearms. A radiation-badge dosimeter clipped at his collar, the window long since gone black.

recruits.name: Kiet Somsak
recruits.backstory: Eleven years a motorcycle courier in Bangkok, which means eleven years of being invisible in traffic and arriving before anyone expected. He went into offices, kitchens and back rooms all day long, and nobody ever looked at him twice. He kept a great deal of what he overheard. Here the skill transfers whole, and he's been careful to let very few people work out that it's a skill.
recruits.greeting: Keep your voice down. Half of what I know, I learned from people who thought nobody was listening.

background_sections.before:
A bike, a bag, and a city where the fastest route changed hourly.

He lived with his grandmother, Yai Boonsri, in Khlong Toei. She was eighty-four and couldn't manage the stairs, so he carried her up and down every day. She called him her legs.
background_sections.adjustment:
It took six weeks. He had a route across the Tanaris desert before he had a bed.

He says the hard part was the quiet. Eleven years of engine noise, and then a world where he can hear people breathing two rooms away.
background_sections.now:
The Abyssal Sands, south of Tanaris, carrying things between the camps faster than anyone else can. Everybody talks near the person carrying something, and nobody watches him.

He's mapped the whole desert by how long each route takes at each hour, which is the first thing he does anywhere, and he's stopped being surprised that nobody else does it.
background_sections.forward:
A standing arrangement with somebody who pays for information and asks for it politely. He's had three offers, and all three were from people he'd rather owe nothing to.

And to stop flinching at silence. Three years in, it's slower going than the rest of it.

recruits.look: Thai man in his late 20s, small and economical in his movements, black hair cut short, a quiet watchful face, hands that are never still. Matte grey-green leathers with a soft hood down, a thin dagger at the small of the back. A brass key blank on a loop of wire at his belt, cut for nothing.

recruits.name: Stelios Dukas
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years a funeral director in Thessaloniki. The trade is composure, paperwork, and being the steadiest person in the worst room of somebody's life. He's unshockable in a way that has nothing to do with callousness, and his profession prepared him for this world considerably better than anybody's did who arrived with a weapon.
recruits.greeting: I handled the dead for nineteen years before any of this. The difference now is that they occasionally have something to add.

background_sections.before:
Arrangements, families, and the particular courtesy of a man who's told four thousand people the worst thing they'll hear that year.

The business was his father's. He's said that inheriting it wasn't a choice, and that he'd have chosen it, and that both of those are true, and that people find the combination difficult.
background_sections.adjustment: He was calm throughout, and he's tired of being praised for it. Composure was his job for nineteen years. You might as well praise a baker for being awake.
background_sections.now:
Glittervein, past the Abyssal Sands, where there are many dead and nobody else to keep records of them.

He does the paperwork. He's extremely good at it, and he's used it four times now to find out who a body was before it stopped being anyone.
background_sections.forward:
Rites, proper ones, for the people from Earth who die here with nobody who knows their language.

He's conducted one hundred and forty. He keeps a register, and he's written to every hub he can reach asking that the names be posted, and three have replied.

recruits.look: Greek man in his early 50s, tall and gaunt, grey hair worn too long, a dry ironic face, half-moon reading glasses on a chain. Charcoal and bone robes with a high collar, a staff topped with a bound sheaf of pages. A librarian's date stamp, brass and wooden-handled, carried in a robe pocket.

recruits.name: Ratih Pranoto
recruits.backstory: Fifteen years a forest ranger in Sumatra, which meant long patrols, poachers, and a government that funded the uniforms and little else. She learned to read a forest for the one wrong thing in it: a snare, a path, a silence where there should be birds. Out on the salt the method is the same, and it's easier to see the wrong thing where nothing hides.
recruits.greeting: You need to walk quieter. I can hear you from the other end of the valley, and so can everything else.

background_sections.before:
A patrol route, a rifle she rarely carried, and the particular loneliness of being the only person in the province who cared.

She has a sister, Dewi, in Medan, and a nephew, Arif, she'd promised to visit that summer. She kept putting it off for one more patrol.
background_sections.adjustment:
She went to work. Within a month she had a patrol route of her own invention and nobody's permission.

The second year was harder, and it was harder for a reason she finds absurd: out here, people thank her.
background_sections.now:
The Shimmering Flats, walking a route she drew herself, looking for the one wrong thing: a trap, a hidden cache, a track that shouldn't be there.

She reports every find to the tauren of Freewind Post and signs none of the reports.
background_sections.forward:
A place on the Freewind guard, properly. Rostered, briefed, part of a line instead of a woman alone on the salt.

She's asked twice. The answers were polite. She's going to ask a third time, and she's decided what she'll say if the answer is the same.

recruits.look: Indonesian woman in her late 30s, slim and weathered, black hair in a tight braid, a direct unsmiling face, fine squint lines. Green and grey leathers with a quiver worn high, a long recurve bow. A brass river-gauge plate, stamped with marks, sewn flat onto her sleeve.

recruits.name: Kourosh Behzadi
recruits.backstory: Twelve years pricing mortality for an insurer in Tehran, the work of establishing, very carefully, how likely a thing is. He finds arcane magic restful by comparison, because for once the numbers hold still. He's calculated a figure he won't tell anybody. The refusal is cheerful rather than grim, and people find that worse.
recruits.greeting: I'm going to stand back here and be extremely precise. You're welcome to be brave. Somebody in a group should be, and it was never going to be the actuary.

background_sections.before:
Tables, reserves, a good office with a bad view, and a mother, Shirin, he telephoned every Friday, who thought the job was beneath him.

She was right that he was capable of more. She was wrong about what more would have meant.
background_sections.adjustment: He arrived mid-calculation and the first thing he did on this world was finish the sum. That was momentum, not bravery, and he's irritated that people keep wanting it to be the other thing.
background_sections.now:
