The Crystalline Underdark, where the crystal lattice does something to arcane magic that nobody has characterised.

He's characterising it, longhand, in a case of notebooks he keeps dry. The case is nearly full.
background_sections.forward:
No journal and no readership, and he's writing it anyway.

He's told two people what's in it. Both changed the subject. He recorded the date each time.

recruits.look: Iranian man in his late 30s, slender and slightly formal in his bearing, black hair neatly cut, close beard, a face that looks faintly amused at all times. Indigo and silver robes with precise geometric trim, a staff of nested rotating rings. A slim mechanical pencil, silver, clipped inside the collar of his robe.

recruits.name: Driss Alaoui
recruits.backstory: Twenty-eight years guiding caravans out of Zagora, across ground where a wrong turn costs a camel and a second wrong turn costs a man. He reads sand the way a sailor reads water. The spirits of the land here needed an introduction, and then settled into something he finds entirely familiar: a long relationship with a landscape that would kill him on a technicality.
recruits.greeting: Water first, then we'll talk about whatever you came here to say.

background_sections.before:
Camels, tourists, and a route his father and his father's father walked before him.

He raised four children on it with his wife Khadija. Three are grown. The fourth, Nour, was nine.
background_sections.adjustment:
He asked the land for permission in his own language and something answered. He mentions this rarely.

The rest of the adjustment was practical: new stars, new seasons, and a year of getting the distances right.
background_sections.now:
Freewind Post, between caravan runs across the canyons of Thousand Needles and the Shimmering Flats, where the goblins pay for a man who gets cargo across intact.

He gets it across. He's refused two contracts over the water allowance, and both parties came back with a better one.
background_sections.forward:
A route across the Shimmering Flats that a caravan can use in summer, when nobody can cross now. There's a way through and he has most of it.

Finishing it means four more seasons of walking, and he has the seasons.

recruits.look: Moroccan man in his mid 40s, lean and long-limbed, black hair greying at the temples under a wrapped headscarf, a narrow thoughtful face. Blue-grey mail and layered cloth with a totem stave and a horn at his belt, static lifting the loose ends of the scarf. A torque wrench, short and stubby, slung in a loop at his hip.

recruits.name: Marisol Quintero
recruits.backstory: Nine years in a Bogotá emergency department, three of them on nights, all of them short-staffed. She learned to keep a frightened person talking while her hands did something they'd rather not watch. The Light and the shadow both move through her easily, and she treats them as instruments on a tray. The habit of narrating came with her, and half the party finds it steadying and half find it maddening.
recruits.greeting: Talk to me while I work, about anything. I do better with a voice in the room, and so do you.

background_sections.before:
Trolleys in a corridor, a triage board, and a city that produced a steady supply.

Her brother Andrés was a motorcycle courier in the same city. She patched him up twice. The second time she shouted at him in the corridor for ten minutes, and she'd give anything to have that back.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eighteen months of working flat out, and she'll tell you honestly that she did it to stay out of her own head.

It worked, and she'd do it again. She knows what it was.
background_sections.now:
Silverpine North, out of the Sepulcher, working the forest road where the wolves and worse take travellers and the Forsaken garrison gets to them slowly.

She reaches them faster. The garrison has noticed, and the quartermaster, apparently, hasn't.
background_sections.forward:
A ward, with four beds, a roof, and somewhere an injured person can lie down for a week instead of being patched up in a field.

There's an empty building at the Sepulcher, and she's been negotiating for it for eleven months with a Forsaken quartermaster who keeps asking whose authority she's under.

recruits.look: Colombian woman in her mid 40s, small and very upright, black hair in a severe low bun, a composed face that reveals nothing at all. Deep violet and black robes with a plain white collar, a slim dark staff, shadow pooling at the hem. A pair of folding reading glasses in a hard case, carried in one sleeve.

recruits.name: Diego Salazar
recruits.backstory: He fixed phones in a mall kiosk in Maracaibo from the age of fifteen, where the power went off twice a day and everybody learned to work in the dark. He can take a thing apart faster than he can explain why. He's one of the few people here who'll say plainly that this world has been good to him, and he won't apologise for it, because the one he left had stopped having anything for him.
recruits.greeting: Ah, you have a broken thing! Give it, give it. No, I'm not guessing, I can hear it. It's the same sound every time, my friend.

background_sections.before:
A folding table, a tray of screws, and a queue.

Four older sisters, all of whom left the country in different years and different directions. He was the last one home and the one who stayed to look after their mother, and he was twenty-two when she died, eight months before the Integration.

So when it happened, he had nobody to lose. He has said that out loud exactly once, and then changed the subject to a gearbox.
background_sections.adjustment:
Three weeks, and he spent two of them delighted.

A goblin handed him a broken pressure valve to see what he would do with it. That is how a goblin asks a question. He had it working before the goblin finished the sentence and has been paid in parts ever since.
background_sections.forward:
A workshop with his name over the door. He'll tell you the exact sign he wants, in two colours, with the lettering slightly crooked because he likes it that way.

He's twenty-five, and nobody has ever talked him out of anything. He won't argue with you about it. He'll smile, say sure, sure, my friend, and do it his way.
background_sections.now:
Wherever there is a pile of broken machinery and somebody willing to let him near it.

He has a half-built clockwork beetle that has been nearly finished for eleven months. Everybody who travels with him has been shown it. Nobody has seen it move.

recruits.look: Venezuelan man in his mid 20s, lean and wiry with quick hands, thick black hair falling over his forehead, dark eyes and a sharp jaw, a bright open good-looking face. Brass-and-canvas tinker's gear, a heavy wrench-hammer at his hip, goggles pushed up on his head. A phone-repair spudger, bright blue plastic scuffed white at the tip, in his breast pocket.

recruits.name: Freja Lindqvist
recruits.backstory: A midwife in Aarhus for six years, mostly nights. The job is being the calmest person in a room where something enormous is happening. She's blunt, and people find it a relief inside about a minute. She's also playful, competitive about everything, and she doesn't back down from anyone. The Light came to her easily and she treats it as a tool, the same as her hands, and she's careful to say so, because she's met two people here who decided they were chosen and she told both of them what she thought of that.
recruits.greeting: You're bleeding and talking at the same time, and you can only do one of those well. Sit down and I'll tell you when you're allowed to start again.

background_sections.before:
Night shifts, a bicycle in every weather, and a flat with too many plants in it.

And William, an American aircraft mechanic who came off his bicycle on the ice outside her hospital. She strapped his wrist on the pavement and told him Americans shouldn't be allowed bicycles. He said Danes shouldn't be allowed opinions. They married two years later and argued about everything, happily. She kept her own name.
background_sections.adjustment:
Steady, on the outside, from the first week.

What she had was a working pair of hands and a world full of people who needed them, and she used that the way you use a railing. She knows exactly what she was doing. She would do it again and recommends it to nobody.
background_sections.forward:
To deliver a baby here. She's said so to three people and watched all three of them fail to understand why it matters to her.

Six years of her life were about the first ninety seconds of somebody else's. She'd like to find out if that still works in a place with this much dying in it.

And there's William. She writes him a letter every week and keeps them in a bundle, because there's nowhere to send them. He's going to read every one.
background_sections.now:
Walking a circuit of the farms and camps, because the fighting gets a healer and the births get whoever is nearest.

She has taught four women to do what she does with their hands when she is not there. That is the part of the work she is proudest of and the part nobody asks her about.

recruits.look: Danish woman in her late 20s, tall and slim with a dancer's posture, long pale blonde hair braided back, grey-blue eyes, fine straight features. White and soft-gold priest robes with a pale blue mantle, a slim silver censer at the belt. A midwife's wooden pinard horn, polished dark with handling, at her side.

recruits.name: Sondre Haugen
recruits.backstory: He taught sailing to teenagers on the Hardangerfjord for four summers and expected to do a fifth. He's good with weather and good with boats, and he was twenty-four and had never had anything bad happen to him. Then the sky here started answering when he spoke to it, and the first time it went wrong it went very wrong, and he's been frightened of himself ever since. He's polite about it, but you can still see it.
recruits.greeting: If I say get down, you get down and you ask me why afterwards. The asking is the part that kills people, and I've seen it happen.

background_sections.before:
A dinghy, a whistle, a clipboard, and a season that ended in August.

His parents and his sister Ingrid are in Bergen, and he has no idea if that means anything now. He talks about them in the present tense, every time, on purpose, like a man holding a door open with his foot.
background_sections.adjustment:
He'll tell you the first year was fine. Anybody who was there will tell you it wasn't.

One afternoon in the second year the wind did something he hadn't asked for, and a barn went over with people inside. Nobody was killed. A girl of about fifteen broke her leg, and he carried her out himself. He hasn't been the same since, and he can't explain why, when nobody died.
background_sections.forward:
Control, and not power. He's got plenty of power, and that's the whole problem.

He's started going out alone to practise where there's nothing to break. The people who care about him think that's the worst possible way to handle it, and they're probably right.
background_sections.now:
The high open ground near the Scarlet Crypt, where he can see weather coming for an hour before it arrives.

He sleeps badly. He's first awake every morning and he's made the fire before anybody else is up, and he offers that as proof he's fine.

recruits.look: Norwegian man in his late 20s, tall and rangy with broad flat shoulders, dark blond hair pushed back and wind-wrecked, pale grey eyes, a weather-reddened face. Storm-blue layered robes with a short cloak that lifts on its own, a long bone-white stave, faint static along his forearms. A sailing-dinghy shackle key on a lanyard at his throat.

recruits.name: Berat Yilmaz
recruits.backstory: A dentist in Izmir, newly qualified, still paying for the chair when the world changed under him. The job is small careful work inside a space the size of a fist, on somebody who'd rather be anywhere else. That turns out to be most of what field medicine asks for. He's wonderful company and he knows it and he uses it, because a frightened patient is a patient who moves.
recruits.greeting: Open your mouth. No, no, I'm joking, I'm joking! It's an old habit. Sit down and let me see the arm.

background_sections.before:
A surgery with his name on the door for eleven months, and a loan with thirty years left on it.

An enormous family, all of them in Izmir, all of them loud. He says he'll find them. He says it the way you say a thing you've decided to believe, and he still says it three years on.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two months, and most of that was the language.

He arrived with better hands than almost anybody and no idea what to do with the rest of himself, so he started asking everyone he met what they used to be. He knows the old jobs of about four hundred people from Earth now, and he'll introduce any two of them who ought to meet.
background_sections.forward:
A proper surgery again, with a door and his name on it, and an apprentice who's frightened of nothing.

He's also keeping a list of everyone from Earth with medical training, because he noticed early that nobody else was, and it's now the only list like it that exists.
background_sections.now:
Wherever the road is busiest, because that's where the broken arms are. Brill, when he sleeps at all.

He still carries the mouth mirror behind his ear. He's used it twice for its real purpose and about forty times to see round a corner.

recruits.look: Turkish man in his late 20s, compact and sturdy, dark curls cut close at the sides, heavy black brows, warm brown eyes, an open face that smiles easily. Copper-plated tinker's coat in oxblood and brass, a backpack of tubes and gauges leaking soft green healing light. A dentist's angled chrome mouth mirror tucked behind one ear.

recruits.name: Matías Fuentes
recruits.backstory: He worked the buses in Chile's capital from nineteen, punching tickets on a route he could have driven blindfolded, in a job his father had before him and thought was beneath his sons. What he's good at is standing still in a crowd of strangers for nine hours and watching all of them at once. He speaks carefully and not much, in English he's built from nothing in three years, and people mistake that for stupidity about twice before they stop.
recruits.greeting: I go in front, it's better that way. You can talk to me after, if you want. Now isn't the time for talking.

background_sections.before:
A route, a fare box, and the same forty faces every morning.

His father died in 2019 and they hadn't spoken in two years. His mother and his little brother were at home. He doesn't talk about any of it, and he's told exactly one person, at night, on watch.
background_sections.adjustment:
Bad, very bad, and he'll say so plainly if asked directly. Almost nobody asks.

He stopped speaking for most of the first year. He didn't mean to. He ran out of things worth the effort of translating, and the quiet got comfortable, and then it got hard to leave.
background_sections.forward:
He's learning to read this world's script, slowly, from a woman at a trade post in Durotar who charges him nothing and corrects him constantly.

He hasn't told anybody why. He wants to write a letter, and he knows there's nowhere to send it, and he wants to write it anyway.
background_sections.now:
At the front, in the Sunken Grotto of the Deep or wherever else is dark, because that's where you can see everybody.

He clicks the ticket punch twice before a fight, every time. Somebody asked him once if it was for luck. He said no and didn't explain.

recruits.look: Chilean man in his late 20s, slim and hard through the shoulders, black hair worn a little long and shoved back, dark eyes, high cheekbones. Charcoal and bone-grey reaper leathers with a hooded half-cape, a long curved scythe-blade carried low, faint violet light at the edge. A bus conductor's brass ticket punch on a cord at his belt.

recruits.name: Giorgi Beridze
recruits.backstory: Twenty years of high summer pasture above Kazbegi, moving sheep up and down a mountain on a calendar his family never wrote down because nobody needed to. He's physically enormous and completely unhurried. His English has grown in three years and he still spends it like money, every word deliberate, and what comes out is often better than what a fluent man would say, because he's got no spare words to hide behind.
recruits.greeting: You walk too fast for the ground, so go slowly. The mountain will wait, and so will you, if you listen.

background_sections.before:
A dog, a herd, a wooden hut, and six months a year without a road.

A wife, Nino, and two daughters in the village below, who he came down to every autumn, and who thought the mountain was an eccentricity he'd grow out of.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two seasons, and he counts in seasons.

The land here needed reading, and he reads land. What took longer was people. On the mountain he spoke to nobody for weeks and that was normal, and here being alone is something other people worry about on your behalf. He finds that exhausting and touching at the same time.
background_sections.forward:
A herd of his own. He's serious, and nobody takes him seriously, and it irritates him more than he lets on.

He's found grazing he says is as good as anything at home, and a tauren herder who argues with him about it. He enjoys that enormously.
background_sections.now:
The high ground above Tarren Mill, where the air is right and the ground tells the truth.

Every autumn, on roughly the right day, he walks down to lower ground for no reason anyone can see. He's never explained it. He's bringing the herd down, and there's no herd.

recruits.look: Georgian man in his mid 30s, big through the chest with heavy forearms, thick dark hair and a short full beard, deep-set hazel eyes. Green and tan hide over mail, a hand-carved totem stave across his back, a hawk's feather bound into it. A shepherd's small dented brass bell, knotted to his belt so it cannot ring.

recruits.name: Camille Roussel
recruits.backstory: For nine years she raced packages across Lyon on a bike, and fixed every other courier's bike too. The job is knowing exactly how much space you have and taking all of it. She's abrasive on purpose, fast, and very funny when she decides to be, and almost nobody gets past the first layer. The ones who do find out she's fiercely loyal, and she'd deny it to your face.
recruits.greeting: You want me to come, fine. But I don't do the thing where we all talk about our feelings at the fire, yes? Good, then we understand each other.

background_sections.before:
A fixed-gear frame she built twice, a radio in one ear, and a city she could cross in twenty-two minutes.

Her brother Théo rode for the same company. He was on the Part-Dieu road that morning and she wasn't, because she'd swapped a shift so she could sleep in. She's said this out loud twice and regretted it both times.
background_sections.adjustment:
She made herself useful immediately and let nobody near her for two years.

It worked, in the sense that she survived it. She knows it wasn't the only option. She says the other options were for people with more patience than her.
background_sections.forward:
She's been mapping the roads between the camps, every one of them, by hand, by riding them, and lately the tunnels of the Wailing Caverns too.

Ask why and she says somebody should. The real answer is that it's the only thing here that feels like the job did, and the job was the last part of her life that worked.
background_sections.now:
On the roads, carrying things between places faster than they've any right to arrive, and in the Wailing Caverns, mapping tunnels nobody else has mapped.

She won't take a message she hasn't read. She found that out the hard way in her second month and has been insufferable about it ever since.

recruits.look: French woman in her early 30s, slim and long-legged, dark brown hair in a thick loose plait over one shoulder, green eyes, elegant features and a faint knowing half-smile. Deep green and oxblood brigand leathers cut close, a hooded short cloak, a long dagger at the hip. A slim silver bicycle-spoke wrench threaded onto her belt.

recruits.name: Orlando Rivera
recruits.backstory: Eleven years cutting hair in Santurce, in a shop that was really the whole neighbourhood's living room. Everybody told him everything, because a barber is a priest with better gossip. He talks constantly and listens harder than anybody notices. The spirits took to him straight away, and he treats them the way he treated his chair. Sit down, tell me what's wrong, and we'll talk the whole time I fix it.
recruits.greeting: Siéntate, siéntate, sorry, in English, sit down, you look terrible, and I say that with love, my friend, with love.

background_sections.before:
Two chairs, a radio always on, and a Tuesday regular called Don Beni who came in for nineteen years and didn't need a haircut once.

His whole family were on the island. He says they're fine. He has a reason he believes it, and he'll tell you the reason, and the reason is thin, and everybody lets him have it.
background_sections.adjustment:
He was running a chair inside a month, in a tent, with a borrowed blade.

It was the most effective adjustment anybody made, and the reason is simple: he rebuilt the room. Everything good he had on Earth came from a place where people sat down and talked, so he made one here before he worried about anything else.
background_sections.forward:
A shop, properly, with a floor and a mirror.

He has the blade. He's had three offers of a building. He's turned all three down and can't explain why to anybody, including himself, and his hands shook on the last one.
background_sections.now:
The Shadowpine Altar on Fenris Isle, where the trolls taught him the spirits and let him keep a chair by the fire. Wherever the party stops becomes a shop for as long as they're there.

He'll cut anybody's hair, any race, free, and nobody's refused him twice.

recruits.look: Puerto Rican man in his early 30s, broad-shouldered and trim, black hair in a short fade, warm brown skin, an easy infectious grin. Bone and indigo witch doctor's gear, feathers and carved charms at the shoulder, a mask pushed up onto his forehead, a gourd rattle at his belt. A barber's pearl-handled straight razor in a sleeve pocket.

recruits.name: Adrián Mendoza
recruits.backstory: A football referee in the Segunda División for eight years, and before that a PE teacher. Two careers of being the least popular person on a field full of people. He is formal, exact and genuinely kind, and the formality is armour he put on so young that he has stopped noticing it. Give him a rule and he will hold it against everybody including himself, and he is the only man in any party who will tell you honestly when you were in the wrong.
recruits.greeting: Tell me the plan once, properly, and I will not ask again. I am not being difficult. I am being useful.

background_sections.before:
Twelve years refereeing in the Segunda División, and before that nine in regional football, which he will tell you was harder.

He lived in Valladolid, in a flat above a cycle shop, and the noise never bothered him. His parents died within a year of each other when he was twenty-eight. No brothers, no sisters. The friendships thinned out the way they do when you work every Saturday and half of Sunday, and he did not chase them.

He says all this the way he would read out a team sheet. Then he asks what you wanted to know.
background_sections.adjustment:
He was useful inside a week, which he found embarrassing.

The first thing he did here was reorganise a supply tent nobody had asked him to touch, and the second was argue with a quartermaster about it for twenty minutes. He won. He has been winning small arguments like that ever since, and apologising for none of them.

What he does not have a reference point for is being wanted in a room. In Valladolid the job was to be ignored. If he was doing it right, nobody said his name all afternoon.
background_sections.now:
Front line, holding whatever line he has been given, which turns out to be close enough to the old job that he is good at it immediately.

He gives the plan once. If you make him give it twice he will, and he will not be pleasant about it. Tarek has pointed out that he could simply be nicer. Adrián said he could, and did not.

He still carries the whistle. It is in the left pocket, always the left, and he pats it when he is thinking. He has never blown it here and would be mortified if anyone noticed how often he checks.
background_sections.forward:
He wants to be invited to something.

He is invited to everything. People come and get him for meals, for watches, for the stupid card game Ama runs, and he goes every time and enjoys himself. But he has never once walked up to a fire and sat down at it without someone waving him over first, and after three years he still waits for the wave.

If you asked him about it he would say he does not want to intrude. He would believe it.

recruits.look: Spanish man in his early 30s, tall and square-shouldered, black hair cut short, close dark beard, a strong jaw. Polished steel and ivory templar plate with a deep red tabard, a one-handed sword and a shield at his back, faint gold light at the seams. A referee's whistle on a black lanyard inside the collar.

recruits.name: Saoirse Ni Bhraonain
recruits.backstory: She played county camogie until her knee went at twenty-six, and then she coached it. The sport is running at people holding a stick and expecting to be run at in return. She's loud, funny and completely without self-pity, and she has an instinct for getting in front of things that predates any of this. Of all of them she's the one most people would want beside them, and she'd find that embarrassing and change the subject.
recruits.greeting: Get behind me and stay there. I know, I know, you're very capable. Humour me and we'll both be alive to argue about it later.

background_sections.before:
A pitch in Kilkenny, a knee that clicked, and a minibus full of fifteen-year-olds she drove to matches at seven in the morning.

No partner, no children, two parents who died within a year of each other, and a brother in Australia she spoke to twice a year out of habit. The girls on the team are the ones she thinks about. She was driving eleven of them to an away match when it happened.
background_sections.adjustment:
Easy, and she's a little ashamed of how easy.

She arrived in a world that wanted somebody to stand in front, and standing in front is the only thing she's ever been unambiguously good at. She's watched people far better than her fall apart while she got on with it, and she has no explanation and offers none.
background_sections.forward:
To coach again, and not to fight.

She's started with four of the youngest at the Sepulcher, teenagers from Earth, on the grounds that somebody has to teach them to fall properly. She runs it at seven in the morning, because that's apparently who she is.
background_sections.now:
The Sepulcher in Silverpine, and Shadowfang Keep wherever the line's thinnest, taking the hits with a cheerfulness other people find unsettling.

The sliotar is still on her belt. She throws it at people who are getting above themselves, underarm and accurately, and the party has learned to catch.

recruits.look: Irish woman in her early 30s, tall and strongly built, long copper-red hair tied back in a heavy knot, pale freckled skin, grey-green eyes. Silver and midnight-blue plate, a round shield with a crescent boss, a short spear, cold moonlight along the armour edges. A hurling sliotar, scuffed and grass-stained, in a net at her belt.

recruits.name: Nicolás Arce
recruits.backstory: Nine years a paramedic in Lima, mostly on motorbikes, because an ambulance can't get through that traffic and a bike can. The work is triage at speed with your hands in somebody's blood, and blood magic asked him for exactly that with the pretence removed. He's steady, unhurried and very hard to frighten, and the one thing that will shut him down completely is being told to leave somebody behind.
recruits.greeting: Stand behind me. If I go down, you run, and you don't drag me. Promise me that now, or find somebody else.

background_sections.before:
A bike, a bag, and a city that produced more work than any crew could finish.

His partner on the bike for six years was Gladys Huamán. She trained him, she swore at him constantly, and she was two streets away when it happened. He's looked for her at every hub he's reached, and he keeps a list of the ones he hasn't reached yet.
background_sections.adjustment:
He worked, and that's the entire answer, and he gives it in those words.

The second year was worse than the first, because by then he'd run out of places nearby to check and had to admit the looking was going to be a long project rather than a short one.
background_sections.forward:
Gladys, obviously, first of all. He won't pretend otherwise and he won't make anybody else carry it.

Beyond that he wants a crew. Two people on a fast thing, going toward what everybody else is going away from. He hasn't found the second person.
background_sections.now:
Splintertree Post in Ashenvale East, and the front of whatever party he's in, soaking what's aimed at the people behind him.

He's the one who notices an hour before anybody else that somebody isn't right. He doesn't announce it. He just ends up walking beside them.

recruits.look: Peruvian man in his early 30s, compact and visibly strong, black hair swept back, dark eyes, high cheekbones. Crimson and black plate worn heavy, a broad shield, a short thick blade, dull red light moving under the plate like something circulating. A paramedic's folding tourniquet windlass clipped at his shoulder.

recruits.name: Ileana Dragomir
recruits.backstory: Second violin in the Cluj philharmonic for eleven years. The job is being corrected in public by a man with a stick, and then doing it exactly right forever after. She's scathing about anything done carelessly and has no patience at all for effort without precision. She's also the first on her feet when somebody goes down, every time, without comment, and the party works that out long before she admits it.
recruits.greeting: That was sloppy, and you know it was sloppy. Do it again properly and I'll stop talking about it, probably.

background_sections.before:
A section, a stand partner, and the particular hell of being very good at something that has four hundred people better.

A husband, Andrei, who taught at the conservatory, and no children, by a decision they made together and both revisited privately. They'd had a bad year and were coming out the other side of it. She describes the year in detail and the coming-out in one sentence, and the one sentence is the part she can't say twice.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two years of being unbearable, by her own account, delivered flatly.

She's precise about her own faults in a way almost nobody is. She drove people off, she knew she was doing it while she did it, and she's apologised to four of them since, one at a time, and been surprised each time that it was accepted.
background_sections.forward:
An ensemble, not an audience. Three or four people who can hold a line while she holds hers.

She's said this once, in a way that made it clear she meant the party, and then immediately criticised somebody's footwork so nobody could answer it.
background_sections.now:
The Undercity, where the cold suits her, and the Plague Depths below it, where the dead are a problem that needs precision. She stands at the back, and the front rank has learned to stand clear of the cold that comes off her.

The shoulder rest is strapped across her back. There's no violin. Nobody has asked her about it twice.

recruits.look: Romanian woman in her mid 30s, slender and very upright, dark brown hair cut in a sharp chin-length bob, pale skin, dark eyes, fine sculpted features. Frost-white and deep grey robes with a high collar, a staff of pale bound bone, breath fogging and rime creeping along her sleeves. A violinist's black curved shoulder rest strapped flat across her back.

recruits.name: Thiago Macedo
recruits.backstory: A physiotherapist in Belo Horizonte who worked mostly with people recovering badly from accidents and strokes. The work is being relentlessly encouraging to somebody who wants to give up and is entitled to. He's huge, gentle and very hard to discourage. The Light came to him in the second year, and the people who know him best say it didn't change him at all, and he agrees, and finds that funny.
recruits.greeting: Hey, hey, look at me. You're not dying today. This I promise you, and I don't promise things.

background_sections.before:
A clinic, a table, and a schedule of people he saw twice a week for months at a time.

A huge family, all on three streets, all in and out of each other's houses. He talks about them constantly and in the present tense. Eleven months ago he saw a cousin's name, Júlio Macedo, on a list at a hub in the south, and he's been walking south in stages ever since, in no hurry, because he's decided it's certain.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eight months, and he spent them being useful to people in a way nobody had asked for.

He was the man who sat with people from Earth in the bad weeks, before anybody organised anything. He still is. He doesn't call it a vocation, and he gets uncomfortable when other people do.
background_sections.forward:
South, eventually, at his own pace, to Booty Bay where the list was.

He's also taught four people how to move an injured body without making it worse, because he watched somebody's back get broken twice: once by a boar and once by the people carrying him away from the boar.
background_sections.now:
Grom'gol, in Stranglethorn, on his way south. In the party he stands in the middle, where he can reach either end of it.

The roll of blue tape is nearly finished. He rations it. He's strapped three people's knees with it, and he'll tell you their names.

recruits.look: Brazilian man in his early 30s, tall and powerfully built, black curls cropped close, warm brown skin, a broad open face with a ready smile. Gold and white paladin plate worn light at the shoulder, a warhammer carried head-down, a soft gold glow around his gauntlets. A physiotherapist's half-used roll of bright blue kinesiology tape in a belt pouch.

recruits.name: Skye Donnelly
recruits.backstory: Eleven seasons with a Country Fire Authority brigade outside Ballarat. It's volunteer work that eats your entire summer and most of your friendships. She knows fire as a thing with moods, and she's the only caster most people have met who treats her own magic as something to be managed rather than owned. She's very funny and swears a great deal and is completely dependable at the moment it matters.
recruits.greeting: Right, stand upwind and don't touch anything that's glowing. That's the whole briefing, and you'll be fine.

background_sections.before:
A tanker, a pager, and a shed with a kettle in it where the crew sat out the nights nothing happened.

Divorced at twenty-nine, amicably, and she'll say the fire brigade was most of the reason and that she'd do it again. Her parents retired to Queensland. She assumes they're fine, on grounds she admits are entirely vibes.
background_sections.adjustment:
She found a fire in her first week and put it out, and says that sorted her head out for a year.

The harder part was finding out she could start one. She's thought about that more than she lets on, and she has a rule she tells nobody, and she's never broken it.
background_sections.forward:
A proper brigade. Actual volunteers, actual training, actual kit, for a world that burns constantly and has nobody organised about it.

She has six people. Four of them turn up. She describes this as going extremely well, and she means it.
background_sections.now:
Wherever the burning is, which in this world is most places. Lately that's the Drowning Floor under Southern Thousand Needles, where something keeps setting the oil seeps alight under the water. A pyromancer in a flooded cave makes everyone laugh, her included.

The helmet torch is still clipped to her belt and the battery died two and a half years ago. She clicks it on out of habit and laughs at herself every time.

recruits.look: Australian woman in her early 30s, athletic and sun-browned, long honey-blonde hair pulled up messily, light blue eyes, freckles. Scorched orange and ash robes cut short at the sleeve, a slim rod wrapped in blackened wire, heat shimmer off her forearms. A firefighter's yellow smoke-stained helmet torch clipped at her belt.

recruits.name: Vuk Jovanović
recruits.backstory: He ran a kafana in Novi Sad that his uncle left him, and he's a far better cook than he is a fighter. He says so himself, with some bitterness. He's blunt to the point of rudeness about small things and completely reliable about large ones. He took to this world badly and is only now coming out of it, and the coming out looks like him feeding people and insulting them while he does it.
recruits.greeting: You cooked this? I'm sorry, but it's terrible. Sit down, I'll show you. No, you sit, it's faster if I do it.

background_sections.before:
A kitchen, a card table, and forty regulars who came for the beans and stayed because there was nowhere else.

A daughter, Mila, who was nine, and an ex-wife, Jelena, he was on decent terms with. They had Mila on alternate weeks. It wasn't his week.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two years that he describes in three words, and nobody presses him on them.

What brought him back was being handed a cooking pot in a camp and being too irritated by how badly it was being used to leave it alone. He's cooked for whoever's nearby ever since, and he still says he isn't a cook any more.
background_sections.forward:
He won't say. He's been asked, and he changes the subject every time, usually to food.

What anyone can see is that he's started keeping a second bowl ready at every meal, without being able to say who he thinks it's for.
background_sections.now:
Rocky Pass, the cleft up to the summit of the Aspen country, at the front with an axe, badly, and at the fire afterwards doing the thing he's actually good at.

He carries a domino from the kafana set, the double six, in his glove. He puts it on the table when he sits down to eat. He's never explained it, and nobody asks.

recruits.look: Serbian man in his mid 30s, very tall and heavy-framed, dark hair shaved close at the sides, pale eyes, an old thin scar through one brow. Black and dull-iron war plate with a torn dark surcoat, a two-handed axe across his back, faint cold green light in the gorget. A cast-iron domino tile, double six, carried in one glove.

recruits.name: Khalid Al Suwaidi
recruits.backstory: He kept falcons outside Al Ain, in a family that had done it for longer than anybody wrote down, and he worked in logistics at the airport to pay for it. The hunting is the part of his old life that transferred whole: the waiting, the reading of ground, and the particular relationship with an animal that's choosing to come back to you. He's dry, extremely funny once you know him, and more at home here than he ever admits in company.
recruits.greeting: Walk where I walk and we'll have a very boring day. That's the aim. Boring is the aim, I can't stress this enough.

background_sections.before:
A mews, a glove, and a saker falcon called Hurra, eleven years old, who he'd flown since she was a fledgling.

A large family, all nearby, all of whom thought the falcons were an expensive eccentricity, and all of whom came out to watch anyway.
background_sections.adjustment:
Three months, and he has the grace to find that funny.

He landed in open country with weather and birds in it and no airport, and he says that if he's honest, the first year was the best he'd had in a decade. He says it quietly, and only to people he's decided won't misunderstand it.
background_sections.forward:
A bird, properly trained, properly flown, not a summoned thing.

He's been working on a nest of something enormous in the hills above the Flats for two seasons, patiently and badly. It's taken food from his hand twice, and twice tried to remove the hand.
background_sections.now:
Saltwheel, the goblin racing town on the edge of the Shimmering Flats. With a party he's out ahead, usually invisible, always exactly where he said he'd be.

The falconer's hood still hangs at his belt. It's sized for a bird that's been dead or alive for three years without him knowing which, and he won't be getting another one that size.

recruits.look: Emirati man in his mid 30s, tall and lean, black hair under a loosely wrapped cloth headscarf, close beard, dark eyes, a hawkish face. Sand, grey and deep red survival leathers with a short cloak, a long recurve bow and a heavy belt knife, traps and cord at his hip. A falconer's small tooled leather hood hanging from his belt.

recruits.name: Karim Haddad
recruits.backstory: A land surveyor out of Amman, fifteen years of standing in empty country deciding where the lines went, mostly alone and entirely content with it. He took the fel deliberately, after consideration, as the fastest route to being useful in a fight, and he'll defend that choice in detail to anybody who raises it. He's cold on first meeting and very dry once he decides you're staying.
recruits.greeting: You're looking at the eyes. Everybody looks at the eyes. Ask the question or stop looking, either's better than this.

background_sections.before:
A tripod, a plumb bob, and weeks at a time in country with nobody in it.

No wife, no children, by preference. His parents are both dead, and his brother Sami moved to Canada in 2011, and they slowly stopped calling. He'll tell you this flatly, because he's noticed people want to be sad on his behalf, and he finds it tiring.
background_sections.adjustment:
He treated it as a survey, a new country, unmapped, and a man whose whole trade is deciding where things are.

He was functioning inside a month, and he's said more than once that having nobody to grieve made it easy, that he knows how that sounds, and that it's still true.
background_sections.forward:
A map, the real one, properly surveyed, of where the transit hubs came down and which places on Earth they took people from, because the hubs make no sense and nobody competent has looked.

He's four years into a job that needs twenty, and he says so without minding.
background_sections.now:
The Undercrust, beneath the Shimmering Flats, and the front of any party, where the green light makes the people behind him uncomfortable and he's stopped apologising for it.

The plumb bob still hangs at his hip. He uses it. The party has learned that when he stops and lets it swing, something ahead is wrong.

recruits.look: Jordanian man in his mid 30s, tall and lean-muscled, black hair cut short, close-trimmed beard, dark eyes with a faint green cast. Dark iron and fel-green plate with heavy pauldrons, a jagged greatsword across the back, green light bleeding from the joints. A surveyor's brass plumb bob on a worn cord at his hip.

recruits.name: Osvaldo Beltrán
recruits.backstory: He played trumpet in a Havana hotel band for sixteen years, six nights a week, for tourists who talked through all of it. He's enormously talented at a thing nobody here has any use for, and that's most of what's wrong with him. His English is better than he lets on, and he still uses as little of it as he can, and he's blunt to the point of rude and has never been unkind about anything that mattered.
recruits.greeting: You want fire, I give you fire. You want conversation, I'm the wrong man.

background_sections.before:
A bandstand, a residency, and a brother on piano, Rubén, who was better than him and knew it.

His mother was ninety-one and lived three streets from the hotel. He went every afternoon before the set. He's said one sentence about her in three years.
background_sections.adjustment:
He stopped playing. There was nothing to play and nobody to play with, and he put it down, and it stayed down.

The fire came after that, and he'll tell you the order matters. He was already empty when he went looking, and he thinks that's the only reason it took.
background_sections.forward:
Nothing he'll admit to.

What anyone can see is that he's twice stayed up all night with people who were in a bad way, saying almost nothing, just sitting there. Both of them told somebody about it. He's denied it both times.
background_sections.now:
Aboard the Bloodsail Raider, the pirates' hired fire, burning ships for people he doesn't care about, and tired of it.

The mouthpiece hangs at his throat. Nobody's seen him use it. Somebody heard him humming once, badly, and had the sense to say nothing.

recruits.look: Cuban man in his late 30s, broad-chested and thick-armed, black hair shaved close, warm brown skin, a heavy-browed face that rarely moves. Scorched black and ember-orange robes with the sleeves burned back, a staff capped in a slowly burning coal, soot on his hands. A trumpet mouthpiece, brass gone dull gold, on a cord round his neck.

recruits.name: Bashir Khalidi
recruits.backstory: A stonemason in Nablus for twenty-two years, in a trade of taking something apart correctly before you rebuild it. He's severe, literal and entirely without small talk, and people read that as coldness for about a week. He hunts corrupted things the way he cut stone: slowly, along the grain, with no interest at all in how long it takes.
recruits.greeting: I'll tell you what I find, all of it, including the parts you'd rather I kept to myself. If that's a problem, say so now.

background_sections.before:
A yard, a chisel, and walls his grandfather worked on before him.

A daughter, Rana, nineteen, who'd just started at the university in Birzeit and told him the week before that she meant to study engineering instead of anything he'd suggested. He'd been pleased, and he hadn't said so yet.
background_sections.adjustment:
He went looking for her immediately and didn't stop for eleven months.

He walked to four hubs in that time, on foot, through country that kills people. He found nothing. He came back, said nothing about it to anybody, and started doing the work he does now.
background_sections.forward:
He's never said. The closest anybody's got is that he keeps a list of the places he hasn't searched, and the list is getting shorter, and he's begun to look at what's at the end of it.

He's told one person that he means to be useful until then. That's the plan.
background_sections.now:
The Drowned Shrine, off Southern Stranglethorn, out at the edge of the corruption with a lantern, where the work is slow and almost nobody volunteers.

He snaps the chalk line before he goes in anywhere. He's done it at every doorway for three years, and he does it without seeming to notice.

recruits.look: Palestinian man in his early 40s, tall and spare with long hard forearms, black hair cut short and grey at the temples, a severe face with a strong nose. Black and bleached-bone leathers under a long storm coat, a heavy crossbow at the hip, a silvered blade, a lantern burning pale white. A stonemason's blue-dusted chalk line reel at his belt.

recruits.name: Gianluca Ferri
recruits.backstory: He ran a bar in Bologna that his parents ran before him, opening at six for the people going to work and closing late for the people avoiding going home. Thirty years of standing behind a counter reading a room. He talks without stopping, he remembers what everybody drinks, and he's defused more fights with a joke than most soldiers have with a weapon. Behind a shield he's immovable, and nobody expected that from the man who won't shut up.
recruits.greeting: You want to go in there? Fine, fine, but we go slowly, you let me go first, and afterwards you buy me something hot. That's the arrangement.

background_sections.before:
A counter, a machine he rebuilt himself twice, and the six o'clock crowd who never ordered because he already knew.

A wife, Ornella, who ran the kitchen and the money and most of him. Two sons, both grown and both in Milan, who rang on Sundays.
background_sections.adjustment:
He built a bar. Not a real one, just a spot by a fire where he stood and people came to him, and he turned that into a job inside four months.

He's said he didn't know what else to do with himself, and that what he actually missed was being the person everyone passes in the morning.
background_sections.forward:
A real bar, with a room, a door and a machine. He describes it constantly and in enormous detail, and he's done nothing about it in three years.

He walks to the hubs every few months. He reads the Bologna list and the Milan list, in that order, and he reads the Milan list twice.
background_sections.now:
Steamwheedle Port, by a fire where the goblins and sailors and caravan guards come to him. In a party he's at the front with a shield, keeping up a running commentary the enemy finds as unsettling as everyone else does.

The brass tamper hangs at his belt. He has no coffee and no machine. He's tried a dozen local substitutes and rated every one out of ten, unkindly.

recruits.look: Italian man in his late 30s, broad and solidly built, dark hair greying at the temples, close beard, brown eyes, a lined face that looks faintly amused. Burnished bronze and deep blue plate, a kite shield, a short stabbing sword, a furled banner behind one shoulder. A barista's brass coffee tamper, handle worn smooth, at his belt.

recruits.name: Elias Peralta
recruits.backstory: A motorcycle mechanic in Santo Domingo who went to church on Sundays because his grandmother expected it, and stayed in the habit after she stopped being able to ask. He's the calmest person in most rooms. The Light arrived in his second year, during nothing in particular, while he was fixing a cart, and he's never presented it as a sign. He treats it as a tool that showed up, and he's been learning its tolerances ever since.
recruits.greeting: Take your time. I've got this side. Nothing's getting past me while you sort yourself out, hermano.

background_sections.before:
A workshop with a tin roof, four bikes in pieces at any time, and a radio he and his cousin Junior argued over.

An enormous family in the capital, and a girlfriend, Yamila, he'd been seeing for two years and hadn't told his mother about, for reasons that seemed important at the time.
background_sections.adjustment:
Slow and undramatic. He fixed things for about eighteen months and let everything else wait.

He'll tell you he coped well, and the people around him agree. He's also said, once, that he thinks he simply hasn't got to it yet, and that it's still sitting somewhere waiting for him.
background_sections.forward:
Something that'll outlast him, and he means a building, not a legacy.

He's drawn up a shelter for a crossing on the coast where travellers get caught out by storms: four walls, a roof and a stove. He's shown the drawing to nobody, because he knows the first question will be who it's for.
background_sections.now:
The Drownbell, on the coast of Northern Tanaris, and the front of any party, taking what's aimed at other people with an air of mild apology.

The inspection mirror lives in his gauntlet. He uses it to see round corners and, more often, to check on the people behind him without turning round.

recruits.look: Dominican man in his early 30s, tall and lean with long limbs, black hair in a short twist-out, dark brown skin, warm dark eyes, a wide calm mouth. White and radiant gold plate with layered feathered pauldrons, a tall tower shield, light collecting above his shoulders. A mechanic's round telescoping inspection mirror in his gauntlet cuff.

recruits.name: Rui Almeida
recruits.backstory: He crewed a sardine boat out of Peniche from the age of sixteen, in a family trade that was collapsing under him the whole time he was in it. He's soft-spoken, apologetic and almost unbearably gentle, and he carries something that frightens him badly. He took it in his first year when the alternative was dying, and he's been paying for it since, and he's never tried to make it sound like a good decision.
recruits.greeting: Please don't ask me what it is. I'll tell you what it does, and that has to be enough, because the rest I can't say out loud.

background_sections.before:
Nights out and mornings in, a hold full of fish, and a co-operative that went from forty boats to nine in his working life.

His mother and his two sisters are in Peniche, and he was the one who sent money. He thinks about the money more than he thinks about them, and he knows that's a strange thing to be ashamed of, and he's ashamed of it anyway.
background_sections.adjustment:
It was catastrophic. He landed alone on the Tanaris coast with a broken leg, and something offered.

He said yes. He hasn't defended that choice to anybody in three years. When people assume the worst about him he lets them, because arguing would mean explaining, and explaining is the part he can't do.
background_sections.forward:
Out, quietly, without anybody making a fuss about it.

He's asked three priests and two shamans, carefully and in general terms, and nobody's given him an answer he believes. He keeps asking. It's the only thing he's stubborn about.
background_sections.now:
The Lashings, on the coast of Northern Tanaris, as close to the sea as he can get. In a party he's behind everyone, extremely effective and visibly uncomfortable about it.

He sleeps nearest the fire. He's never said why, and nobody's worked out that it isn't the cold.

recruits.look: Portuguese man in his mid 30s, slim and a little gaunt, dark hair worn loose to the jaw, deep-set dark eyes, hollow cheeks. Deep violet and black robes with a torn high collar, a thin crooked staff, shadow pooling and moving wrongly around his feet. A fisherman's salt-bleached wooden net needle through his belt.

recruits.name: Nizar Haddad
recruits.backstory: A mathematics teacher three times over, with eleven years in Homs, then six in Beirut, then four in Hamburg in a language he was still learning. He's rebuilt his life three times, and this is simply the fourth. He says so without any self-pity, and most people from Earth go quiet when they hear it. His English is careful and slightly old-fashioned, learned from books and the BBC, and he's more precise in it than most people born to it.
recruits.greeting: A moment, if you'd permit me. I should like to understand the sequence before we add ourselves to it.

background_sections.before:
A blackboard, forty students, and the particular patience of a man explaining the same proof for the ninth time without letting it show.

His wife Lamia died in 2016, before any of the rest of it. His daughter Hala was twenty-two and studying in Amman, and they spoke every single day, and he can tell you the time of the last call.
background_sections.adjustment:
Better than almost anyone, because he'd done it before and knew the shape of it.

He's said that the first time you lose everything it destroys you, the second time it's merely very hard, and the third time you find you have a method. He doesn't offer this as wisdom. He offers it as information, to people who look like they need it.
background_sections.forward:
To find his daughter. He's systematic about it in a way that's painful to watch: hub by hub, list by list, in a notebook, with dates.

He's also started teaching again, four children in a trade post at Booty Bay, mathematics, in the evenings, for nothing. He says it's to keep his hand in.
background_sections.now:
Aboard the Crossing, the ship between Booty Bay and the other continent, because from it he can reach the most hubs. In a party he's at the back, holding the order of things together while the front rank works.

His father's watch runs backwards on its chain. He's never had it mended. He winds it every morning regardless, and he hasn't explained that to anybody.

recruits.look: Syrian man in his early 40s, tall and very upright, black hair greying at the sides, neat beard, dark eyes, deep laugh lines. Pale sand and deep teal robes with layered geometric trim, a staff of slowly counter-rotating brass rings, faint afterimages trailing his hands. A pocket watch with a cracked crystal, running backwards, on a fine chain.

recruits.name: Yusuf Al-Rawi
recruits.backstory: A pharmacist in Basra for nineteen years, in a shop where half the job was medicine and the other half was listening to people with no money for a doctor. He knows doses and he knows poisons. He's very warm, and he won't sugarcoat anything for you.
recruits.greeting: Sit, sit, please. You're not dying, I can see that from here. But you'll sit anyway, because I'm older than you.

background_sections.before:
A counter, a wall of drawers, and a queue that was also a social occasion.

A wife, Suhad, three sons and a daughter, and a house with too many people in it and a flat roof they all slept on in the summer. He talks about them easily and often, in the present tense, and nobody's heard him guess at where they are.
background_sections.adjustment:
He was calm about it. He found the work and did it, the way he'd found work in two other countries already.

He's one of the very few here who says plainly that he expects to see his family again, and he says it so calmly that people believe him.
background_sections.forward:
A proper dispensary, with shelves, drawers and labels, and somebody trained to run it when he's out.

He's teaching two people to read the labels he writes, so the place can keep going without him.
background_sections.now:
The Bloodsail Anchorage, where the pressed crews and prisoners are sick and nobody else will treat them. The pirates put up with him because he treats them too.

In a party he's at the back with a bandolier of vials, dosing by eye and not by guess. The brass counting tray is strapped flat on his back, and his numbers are always right.

recruits.look: Iraqi man in his early 40s, broad and heavy-set but light on his feet, black hair receding and swept back, thick moustache and short beard. Dark green and gold robes with wide sleeves, a serpent-carved stave, corked vials in a bandolier across his chest. A pharmacist's scratched brass pill-counting tray slung flat at his back.

recruits.name: Rhys Morgan
recruits.backstory: Rhys flew hawks at weddings in the Brecon Beacons, which paid better than you'd think and was mostly about keeping a bird calm in front of two hundred people in hats. He had Tegan on his glove the evening the world changed, and she crossed over with him. He's quiet, patient and quick to laugh once he's decided you're all right, and he trusts the hawk's opinion of a stranger more than his own.
recruits.greeting: Keep your voice down near the trees, would you? She hunts better when nobody's chattering at her.

background_sections.before:
A falconry centre outside Brecon, weddings in the summer and school visits in the winter.

His mam ran the café at the centre and called every bird by the wrong name on purpose.
background_sections.adjustment:
Tegan adjusted faster than he did. She found the first hare in Stonetalon inside a week, and he decided that if she could manage, he could too.

He still checks the sky for weather the way he did at home, and here it's usually right.
background_sections.forward:
Word to Brecon, or to find out there's no Brecon to send it to.

Until then he's teaching a tauren boy from Sun Rock Retreat how to hold a glove, and the boy is better at it than he was.
background_sections.now:
Out on the western ridges of Stonetalon, where the hunting is good and the road is quiet.

Tegan sits on his arm while he talks and watches whoever he's talking to.

recruits.look: Welsh man, 30, lean and athletic, dark brown wavy hair cut short, light stubble, grey-green eyes. Green and brown ranger leathers with a short hooded cloak, a longbow, a hunting horn, a hawk on a leather gauntlet, a falconer's swivel and bell on a cord round his wrist.

recruits.name: Gunnar Sigurðsson
recruits.backstory: Gunnar brewed beer in Akureyri, in a shed behind his uncle's garage that grew into a proper brewery with a queue out the door on Fridays. He's enormous, loud and generous, and he took to the barbarians of the north the moment he met them, because anyone who toasts their ancestors before a fight has the right idea about both. He still carries a hydrometer, and he still uses it.
recruits.greeting: You look like someone who's had a long road. Sit down, I've got something you should try.

background_sections.before:
A brewery, a dog called Brúnó, and a long-running argument with his sister about whether stout counts as food.

He played second row for a rugby club that lost almost every match and celebrated every one anyway.
background_sections.adjustment:
He landed in snow in the north, which helped. A clan took him in after he fixed their mead, and he's been fixing it since.

He cried once, the first time he heard their ancestor songs, and he doesn't mind who knows it.
background_sections.forward:
He's after a barley that'll grow on the Arathi moor, because the stuff in Hammerfall's stores isn't fit for pigs.

He'd like to brew something good enough that the orcs stop pretending they don't like it.
background_sections.now:
In Hammerfall, by the inn, swapping recipes with Grettha and losing most of the arguments.

The keg on his back is never quite empty, and nobody has ever seen him fill it.

recruits.look: Icelandic man, 37, very big and broad, long dark-blond hair tied back, a thick braided beard, pale blue eyes. Fur-trimmed barbarian hides over mail, a two-handed axe across his back and a small wooden keg on a strap, a brass hydrometer in a leather sleeve on his belt.

recruits.name: Réka Farkas
recruits.backstory: Réka made stop-motion films in Budapest, moving puppets one frame at a time until they looked alive. She'd done it for twelve years when the worlds joined, and it turned out to be the best training for necromancy anyone's ever had. She's sly, funny and very precise, and she treats the dead the way she treated her puppets, with patience and a lot of small adjustments.
recruits.greeting: Don't stare at the crow, it's shy. Well, it was shy. Now it's mostly bones and opinions.

background_sections.before:
A studio above a bakery in the eighth district, and a short film that won a prize in Annecy.

She lived alone with a cat that hated every puppet she ever made.
background_sections.adjustment:
The first time she raised something, she said she knew exactly where she'd gone wrong with the elbow.

The people on the Black Strand don't like what she does, but they like that she's tidy about it.
background_sections.forward:
To make something move that's never moved before, and she's careful not to say what.

She's also looking for a good camera. She knows there isn't one, and she keeps looking anyway.
background_sections.now:
On the Black Strand, in the black sand under the Dry Deep, raising crows out of whatever the beetles leave.

The little mannequin on her belt is the last thing she animated at home, and it still has the wire in its arm.

recruits.look: Hungarian woman, 30, slim, glossy dark chestnut hair to her shoulders with a heavy fringe, pale skin, large dark-hazel eyes. Charcoal and bone-white necromancer robes with a high collar, a staff of bound bone, a small raised skeletal crow on her shoulder, a tiny wooden artist's mannequin on her belt.

recruits.name: Ramiro Quispe
recruits.backstory: Ramiro mined silver in Potosí, in the Cerro Rico, like his father and his grandfather, and he learned young that the mountain talks before it moves. He's steady, proud and quietly funny, and the Dark Iron of Onyxhollow took to him because he hears the rock the way they do. The earth answers him now, which he says is only fair after all the years he spent listening to it.
recruits.greeting: Listen, really listen. You can hear the rock settling. This town's built on good stone.

background_sections.before:
Twelve-hour shifts, a cooperative that never paid on time, and a wife who ran a juice stall in the market.

He has two daughters, and the elder wanted to be a geologist. He was saving for it.
background_sections.adjustment:
He landed underground, which was the one thing that made sense.

The first stone that lifted itself into his hand frightened him badly. He's used to it now, mostly.
background_sections.forward:
To find out whether Potosí crossed over too, and whether anyone is still underneath it. His whole shift was in the mine with him.

In the meantime he's teaching the Onyxhollow apprentices to timber a drift the way his father did, and they've stopped laughing at the method.
background_sections.now:
In Onyxhollow, in the mining quarter, mostly listening.

The carbide lamp on his belt hasn't had fuel in three years. He keeps it polished anyway.

recruits.look: Bolivian man, 36, compact and powerful, black hair cropped short, warm brown skin, dark eyes. Primalist plate studded with raw stone in grey and ochre, a stone-headed stave, pebbles floating above his open hand, a dented brass carbide headlamp strapped to his belt.

recruits.name: Graham Ashworth
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years of night shifts at a hospice outside Preston taught Graham that a slow ending can be a kind one, if somebody pays attention. Affliction came to him easily, and that bothered him more than anything else here, until he worked out it's the same patience pointed the other way. He's gentle, tired and very good company.
recruits.greeting: Sit down a minute if you need to. Most people who come up this road do, and there's no shame in it.

background_sections.before:
Night shifts at a hospice outside Preston, and a garden he never had time for.

His husband Tom taught music at the primary school and sang in the car whether Graham liked it or not.
background_sections.adjustment:
He spent the first year nursing whoever needed it, and the second year learning why the Forsaken didn't.

When he found out what he could do with shadow, he sat with that for a long while before he used it.
background_sections.forward:
He's looking for Tom. He goes through the lists at every town he passes and he hasn't missed one yet.

He'd also like a garden, and the Pale Watch has a corner of ground he's been eyeing.
background_sections.now:
At the Pale Watch, where the plague comes up close and slow, which he understands better than most.

The watch pinned upside down on his chest still runs. He winds it every morning before anything else.

recruits.look: English man, 41, tall and fit, light brown hair going silver at the temples, light beard, blue-grey eyes. Dark violet and sickly green affliction robes with a long scarf, a staff with a cracked lantern, faint green motes, a nurse's fob watch pinned upside down on his chest.

recruits.name: Elie Khoury
recruits.backstory: Elie drew blood for a living at a clinic in Achrafieh, and he was the one the nervous patients asked for. He arrived here with a tourniquet in his pocket and found out that blood listens to him now. He heals with it, which most bloodmages think is a waste and he thinks is the only sensible use. He's calm, warm and careful, and very hard to rattle.
recruits.greeting: Give me your arm. I promise this is the least frightening thing you'll see in Khaz Varun.

background_sections.before:
The clinic, his mother's cooking every Sunday, and a motorbike he kept running on spare parts and faith.

He was saving to go to medical school in Montpellier. He'd been saving for six years.
background_sections.adjustment:
The first time he felt someone's blood move under his hand, he finished the job before he let himself be frightened.

He says the work is the same as it ever was, he just doesn't need the needle.
background_sections.forward:
Teaching other people to heal his way. The Ashclaim's healers keep asking, and he keeps saying yes.

He'd also like to see the sea again. He grew up beside it.
background_sections.now:
In the upper halls of Khaz Varun, patching up whoever comes out of the dark worse than they went in.

The blue needle cap clipped to his sleeve is from the last blood draw he did at home. He's never taken it off.

recruits.look: Lebanese man, 33, slim and neat, black hair swept back, close trimmed beard, dark eyes. Crimson and black bloodmage robes over light mail, a short ritual knife and a slim staff, red threads of light at his fingers, a tourniquet band and a blue butterfly-needle cap clipped to his sleeve.

recruits.name: Bruno Teixeira
recruits.backstory: Bruno fought heavyweight in Curitiba, in small halls with loud crowds, and he was better at it than his record says. He joined the Scarlet Crusade in the first months because it was the only army winning, and he walked out of it beside Rory Callahan the night they burned the transplant camp. He's huge, cheerful and very hard to knock down, and he fights like the bell's about to go.
recruits.greeting: Rory says I smile too much for a templar. I tell him somebody in the Order has to.

background_sections.before:
A gym above a tyre shop, a coach called Seu Valdir, and twenty-three fights with eighteen wins.

His mother came to every fight and covered her eyes for all of them.
background_sections.adjustment:
He says the Crusade took him in and taught him the Light, and that's the part he kept.

The rest he left on the road out of Hearthglen, and he doesn't talk about that night unless Rory does first.
background_sections.forward:
He wants the Order to be big enough that nobody has to choose between the Crusade and nothing again.

He's also teaching the Bulwark's recruits to fight with their hands, and he's delighted with all of them.
background_sections.now:
In the Order's quarter of the Bulwark, training anyone who'll stand in front of him.

The roll of black hand-wrap on his belt is from his last fight at home. He won it.

recruits.look: Brazilian man, 34, huge through the chest and shoulders, short dark brown hair, light olive skin, short dark beard, warm brown eyes. Grey steel templar plate with a white tabard bearing a pale flame, a two-handed warhammer with white holy fire, a roll of black fighter's hand-wrap tucked in his belt.

recruits.name: Joaquín Duarte
recruits.backstory: Joaquín taught history at a secondary school in Rosario until the Integration. In the Crusade they made him an interrogator, because he was patient and he listened, and he was good at it in a way he'll be sorry for until he dies. He left with Rory Callahan. Now he heals with the same hands, and he fights with them too, and he carries what he did there without asking anyone to carry it for him.
recruits.greeting: If you've got something heavy to put down, the Order's a good place to do it. I'd know.

background_sections.before:
A classroom of fifteen-year-olds, a mate gourd on his desk, and a novel he'd been writing for nine years.

He was good with the difficult kids, because he listened to them.
background_sections.adjustment:
He says he adjusted too well, and that's the whole problem.

Rory found him in a cell in Hearthglen at four in the morning, sitting with a prisoner he'd been told to break, and they walked out together.
background_sections.forward:
He's writing down the names of everyone he questioned. He wants to find the ones who lived and say he's sorry to their faces.

He's found four so far. Two of them hit him, and he says they were right to.
background_sections.now:
At the Bulwark with the Order, healing the hurt that come in from the Plaguelands.

The mate gourd at his hip is the one from his classroom desk, and he still drinks from it every morning.

recruits.look: Argentine man, 38, tall and lean, dark hair a little long and swept back, close dark beard, dark eyes, a handsome haunted face. Grey mail over a white undercoat with a pale flame on the chest, hands wrapped for fist-fighting, sun-gold light at his knuckles, a worn leather mate gourd and silver bombilla at his hip.

recruits.name: Astrid Nyström
recruits.backstory: Astrid photographed the aurora above Kiruna for tourists and magazines, and spent most of her twenties lying in snow waiting for the sky to do something. She arrived here on a clear night with her camera round her neck, and the stars answered her within the week. She hunts by starlight in North Felwood now. She's calm and bright and very good at waiting for the right moment.
recruits.greeting: Clear nights are the best ones up here. The stars are wrong, but they're very bright.

background_sections.before:
Kiruna, a cabin with no road to it in winter, and a camera worth more than her car.

She had a brother in Stockholm who called every Sunday to ask if she was still alive.
background_sections.adjustment:
The camera stopped working, which she found harder than anything else.

The Sentinels at Talonbranch taught her the bow, and the stars taught her the rest.
background_sections.forward:
She's mapping the new sky, star by star, in a notebook the size of a brick.

She'd like to find her brother's Sunday call again. She knows it's not likely, and she keeps the habit anyway.
background_sections.now:
In North Felwood, out near the Talonbranch camp, hunting what comes out of the fel when the light's low.

The lens cap round her neck belongs to a camera that hasn't worked in three years.

recruits.look: Swedish woman, 32, slim and athletic, long platinum-blonde hair in a loose braid, pale skin, ice-blue eyes. Silver and midnight-blue sentinel leathers, a tall bow strung with faint starlight, star motes along the arrows, a small camera lens cap on a cord round her neck.

recruits.name: Luka Perić
recruits.backstory: Luka captained a car ferry between Split and the islands for fifteen years, and he knows the sea well enough to be properly afraid of it. The storm found him on the crossing, and it's been following him since. He calls it up now on the Tempest Shallows, carefully, the way he used to read the weather off the Adriatic. He's wry, weathered and the steadiest person in any room.
recruits.greeting: Ever seen a squall come in over open water? I have. Stand behind me and you'll be fine.

background_sections.before:
A ferry called the Marjan, a crew of eight, and a wife who ran a konoba on Brač.

His son played water polo, badly, and Luka never missed a match.
background_sections.adjustment:
He woke up on a beach with the ferry's whistle in his hand and no ferry.

The first storm he called up nearly drowned him, and he says that's how he knew it was his.
background_sections.forward:
A boat of his own, small and sound, and he'd take it home if he knew which way home was.

Until then he's teaching the Ashclaim's crews to read the weather before it reads them.
background_sections.now:
On the Tempest Shallows, near the landing, watching the sky.

The brass whistle on his lanyard is from the Marjan's bridge, and he blows it once every evening at the time the last ferry used to leave.

recruits.look: Croatian man, 39, tall and broad-shouldered, short dark hair with some grey, short beard, sea-blue eyes. Deep sea-green and storm-grey robes with a short cloak that drips water, a driftwood staff bound in silver, frost and spray at his feet, a brass ship's whistle on a lanyard.

recruits.name: Zofia Nowak
recruits.backstory: Zofia answered phones for an insurance company in Łódź, eight hours a day of people shouting at her about things she couldn't fix. The Cult of the Damned found her in the first winter and promised her that she'd never be powerless again, and for a while they kept the promise. Then she saw what it cost, and she walked out of Andorhal with what they'd taught her. She's guarded and determined, and nobody talks down to her twice.
recruits.greeting: I know what these robes look like. I tore their symbols off myself, so you can stop staring.

background_sections.before:
A call centre, a flat with her grandmother, and a night course in accounting she was two exams from finishing.

Her grandmother taught her to play cards and cheated every single time.
background_sections.adjustment:
She'd rather not talk about the first year, and she'll tell you that plainly.

She left Andorhal at night, alone, and she took three of the Cult's books with her.
background_sections.forward:
She wants every Cult house in the Plaguelands burned, and she knows where most of them are.

After that she'd like to finish the accounting course, and she's not joking.
background_sections.now:
In the north of the Western Plaguelands, near Andorhal, hunting the people who recruited her.

The headset clip pinned to her collar is from her desk at the call centre, and she wears it like a medal.

recruits.look: Polish woman, 29, slender, long dark-brown hair loose past her shoulders, pale skin, dark eyes, a serious face. Deep violet and black shadow robes with the Cult's symbols torn off and the stitches showing, a thin dark staff, shadow at her fingertips, a black plastic headset clip pinned to her collar.

recruits.name: Sherif Gamal
recruits.backstory: Sherif did pest control in Cairo, fumigating apartment blocks and restaurants and once, memorably, a museum storeroom. He's spent his whole working life very calm around things that sting, and the Royal Hive is full of them. He arrived with his fumigation rig on his back and found out venom listens to him here. He's unbothered, amused and the only person who walks into the hive without flinching.
recruits.greeting: Don't swat at them. Things that sting only get worse when you panic, and they can tell.

background_sections.before:
A van, a fogging machine, and a family business his father started in 1987.

He was engaged to a pharmacist called Mariam, and the wedding was set for the spring after.
background_sections.adjustment:
He says the bugs here are bigger, and otherwise it's the same job.

He means it as a joke, and he also means it.
background_sections.forward:
He's studying the hive's poisons, all of them, because a poison you understand is half an antidote.

He's looking for Mariam. He asks every healer he meets, because she'd have ended up near the sick.
background_sections.now:
Inside the Royal Hive, in the first chambers, cataloguing what lives there.

The brass nozzle hanging from his belt came off his old fogging rig, and he still checks it for blockages.

recruits.look: Egyptian man, 35, medium build and very fit, short black hair, trimmed beard, dark eyes, a calm face. Dark green and sand venomancer robes with a hooded mantle, glass vials and spore pods on a bandolier, a staff with a coiled serpent, a brass fumigation nozzle hanging from his belt.

recruits.name: Santiago Ríos
recruits.backstory: Santiago tattooed in Medellín, in a shop in Laureles with a waiting list that ran for months. He arrived with the grip of his machine in his pocket, and runes started showing up in his work within the month. He engraves them into his blades now, and into his own arms, and they burn when he fights. He's confident, bright and a perfectionist about line work in a way that makes the Ashclaim's smiths nervous.
recruits.greeting: Every rune's a line you can't take back. Same as a tattoo, really, just a lot louder.

background_sections.before:
A shop with his cousin, three hundred clients' worth of designs in a folder, and a little brother he was putting through school.

His mother never approved of the tattoos and had a small one done anyway, by him.
background_sections.adjustment:
